#84. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words)

American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated.
  • View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):.
  • Sources indicate that so this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only highlighted up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):.

Sources indicate that so this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

In a recent development, it’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

It has been revealed that american had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Sources indicate that under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

#83. Delta Air Lines Is Already Flying The Replacement For Its Aging Airbus A319s, But American & United Don't Have One

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Delta Air Lines Is Already Flying The Replacement For Its Aging Airbus A319s, But American & United Don't Have One

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wikimedia Commons, Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying.
  • According to recent reports, american Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines all operate the Airbus A319.
  • The US carriers need to replace these aircraft soon, yet two out of the three haven't ordered the Airbus A319neo, Boeing 737 MAX 7, Airbus A220, or Embraer E2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wikimedia Commons, Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying.

According to recent reports, american Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines all operate the Airbus A319. Together, the three operate over 250 examples, using it as a core aircraft slotting above their regional jets and underneath their larger narrowbodies. However, the aircraft is also old, having debuted in 1996.

The US carriers need to replace these aircraft soon, yet two out of the three haven't ordered the Airbus A319neo, Boeing 737 MAX 7, Airbus A220, or Embraer E2. Delta Air Lines has ordered 145 Airbus A220s, split between 45 A220-100s and 100 A220-300s. The 109-seat A220-100s are much smaller than an A319-100 and are really sized closer to the airline's Boeing 717-200s.

Sources indicate that the 130-seat A220-300s, however, are almost perfectly sized to replace the 132-seat A319-100s. The other airlines have not ordered this aircraft, nor any others to replace their A319s (as well as the 737-700 in the case of United). However, they might not need these planes to replace the A319-100.

Sources indicate that delta first ordered the A220 back in 2016 when the aircraft was still being sold by Bombardier as the CSeries. At the time, the CSeries was a promising plane, but orders were relatively scarce, and Bombardier was desperate to break into the US market in particular. The original order consisted of 75 CS100s (now the A220-100), and Delta received the planes at such an attractive price that it prompted Boeing to file an anti-dumping petition, which was later overturned.

Delta got an amazing price for these planes that is unlikely to be matched. The aircraft is, of course, excellent for its intended missions, but capital cost plays a huge part in the economics of acquiring and operating an aircraft type. The circumstances of the order make the A220 more compelling for Delta than it would be if American or United ordered the type simply because they would need to pay more money.

Sources indicate that this is especially true when considering that it would come with high integration costs. Delta has experienced excellent results with the A220, and has since added 70 orders in total. While the original order solely consisted of 75 CS100s/A220-100s, all subsequent orders have been for the A319-sized A220-300.

Meanwhile, the airline has converted 30 A220-100 orders to the larger variant. While the A220-100 is a competent aircraft in its own right, the A220-300 has more seats without burning significantly more fuel, and the aircraft doesn't even have a significant range penalty for most airlines' purposes.

According to recent reports, while the US airlines operate large fleets of last-generation small widebodies, American and United have not ordered any current-generation examples. However, this is because their replacement for the A319-100 is the A321neo and the 737 MAX 10. Both airlines have been upgauging because the A321neo and 737 MAX 10 offer significantly better per-seat economics than other narrowbody aircraft.

Recent findings suggest that this makes them much more compelling to operate than their smaller counterparts. American Airlines has ordered 206 A321neos in total while also acquiring ten used examples, and it's ordered 115 737 MAX 10s. United Airlines has ordered 210 A321neos, 224 737 MAX 9s, and 167 737 MAX 10s. Both airlines have also ordered the 737 MAX 8, but in smaller numbers (103 for American and 123 for United).

It has been revealed that what will actually happen is the fresh large narrowbodies will take over the carrier's highest demand routes, displacing smaller aircraft down the network and sending the A319-100s to the scrapyard. Delta has done this exact thing, ordering 100 737 MAX 10s and 189 A321neos. While it is taking new A220s, these aircraft are not necessarily replacing the A319-100s one for one.

Industry observers note that instead, Delta will again use its newly introduced large narrowbodies to take over its busiest routes, which will displace other aircraft, including the A220s in some cases. Meanwhile, the A319-100s will go away. For all three airlines, it's their large narrowbodies that will enable displacements throughout the network.

Over the past 15 years, Delta has ordered 145 A220s, while it also leased 88 717s from Southwest Airlines for an exceptionally low price. American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s fresh from Airbus. Otherwise, all of Delta's narrowbody orders have been for the A321-200, A321neo, 737-900ER, and 737 MAX 10. American has otherwise only ordered the A321-200, A321neo, 737-800, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 10.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, United has only taken the A321neo, 737-800, 737-900ER, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 9, while holding orders for the MAX 10. There has been a noticeable trend of US airlines favoring larger narrowbodies, and even the mid-size 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s have fallen out of favor.

According to recent reports, these aircraft simply deliver superior economics to the shrinks in their families, as the added fuel burn is far outweighed by their increased revenue potential. The tradeoff is shorter range and runway performance, but only a handful of mainline stations have truly challenging conditions. At the same time, the A320neo and 737 MAX families have solved the performance and range problems.

Across the board, US airlines are upgauging, switching to larger aircraft for short-haul flights. In the past, another reason why airlines would buy smaller aircraft is to right-size capacity, but the US legacy carriers have strongly employed fare segmentation as a core commercial strategy.

This has reduced the need to operate smaller narrowbodies, since releasing various numbers of differently priced tickets can help fill planes on slower days. This is something that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby has publicly commented on.

It has been revealed that fare segmentation and basic economy fares mean that his airline no longer requires a small narrowbody to meet demand, allowing United to standardize on larger, more economical aircraft. Tellingly, United ordered 45 737-700s in 2016, added another 20 units, then converted all orders to the 737-800 and 737 MAX 9 later the same year.

American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s upcoming from Airbus, while also acquiring a handful of used examples. United Airlines converted all of its later 737-700 orders to larger variants, while also acquiring a handful of used A319-100s. Delta, on the other hand, ordered 145 A220s while also acquiring 88 717s. Of course, the capital costs play a huge role in this.

Industry observers note that specifically, the 717s were essentially a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity due to Southwest's acquisition of AirTran, which originally owned the planes, while the A220s were sold at very low prices. However, another benefit of the small narrowbodies to Delta comes from its pilot agreement.

Industry observers note that the agreement stipulates scope clauses, which place limits and restrictions on regional jet flying contracted out to other airlines under the Delta Connection brand. The largest planes that may be flown for Delta Connection are 76-seaters, and there are hard limits on how many of these planes Delta may operate under the Delta Connection, as they are more economical than 70-seaters or 50-seaters.

In a recent development, delta's scope agreement, however, allows the airline to add additional 76-seaters if it adds a new small mainline narrowbody. The 717s, in addition to being cheap to acquire, unlocked additional 76-seaters for the Delta Connection brand. The A220 order did the same thing, and this is a significant benefit given the scale of the regional operations run by the US airlines. However, this was also a very specific set of circumstances that, combined, made the two purchases work for Delta.

These airlines are the world's three largest operators of the type.

Sources indicate that an opportunity like the 88 717s that Southwest was looking to offload rapidly was only going to occur once, as is also the case for the pricing on Delta's initial A220 order. Beyond this, American Airlines specifically does not have a trigger in its scope clauses for additional 76-seaters if it acquires a upcoming small narrowbody type. Rather, the size of the 76-seater fleet is tied directly to the airline's overall mainline fleet size.

In a recent development, for American, the aircraft has to have merit on its own, and that's difficult to justify. United Airlines does have the same trigger clause as Delta, which means that acquiring an aircraft type sized like the A319-100 would unlock additional 76-seaters. However, the carrier is at the moment focused on substantial network-wide growth through frequency increases and upgauging.

Buying 100+ A220s does not fit its general strategy today, especially considering United's current order book, which is dominated by larger aircraft variants. For both airlines, there is less benefit to acquiring the A220 or a similar small narrowbody aircraft type like Delta has.

Industry observers note that apart from the unique circumstances that made the 717s and A220s attractive to Delta, however, the Atlanta-based carrier is also practicing upgauging and is noticeably doing so throughout the network. The carrier has also shied away from the 737 MAX 8, and there's a distinct possibility that it may simply not order this variant at all.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Definitely would be cool to see an A220-300 in UA colors, but I honestly wonder if they won’t order a replacement due to their preference for larger aircraft.

#81. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

📅 24 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words)
General 🌐 Nomadicmatt

Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Source: Nomadicmatt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road.
  • Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).
  • Sources indicate that but, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

Sources indicate that but, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Industry observers note that currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in fresh destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

Recent findings suggest that it’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

In a recent development, every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

According to recent reports, every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Sources indicate that plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

Sources indicate that and the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

According to recent reports, first, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

It has been revealed that the shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!).

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

It has been revealed that however, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

According to recent reports, at Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

It has been revealed that first, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like Upcoming York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

According to recent reports, can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy concerns).

Sources indicate that living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing latest cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Industry observers note that outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

Etihad Guest has just rolled out its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus.

Recent findings suggest that between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:.

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Sources indicate that etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

Recent findings suggest that as you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Industry observers note that etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Recent findings suggest that below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

Sources indicate that if you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

According to recent reports, etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:.

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Recent findings suggest that everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

Recent findings suggest that of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt presently has 38 brands, which are as follows:.

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Breaking: 17 Best Airbnbs in Bangkok for Your Next Trip to Thailand's Capital

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A vast metropolis where modern skyscrapers mix with antique wooden houses, Bangkok is, in my opinion, one of the best cities in the world.
  • Over the years, I’ve spent months in Thailand’s capital city.
  • We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A vast metropolis where modern skyscrapers mix with antique wooden houses, Bangkok is, in my opinion, one of the best cities in the world. Whether you’re on the hunt for boat noodles or Thai massages, there’s so much to do and no bad time of year to visit. And when it comes to where to stay, travelers will find just as much variety among the excellent lodging options. While this Thai city delivers a sensory overload of epic proportions, there are plenty of peaceful pockets and quiet corners perfect for catching your breath after a long day of exploring. One of the best ways to get a bit of solitude is by renting a dreamy Airbnb in the area.

Over the years, I’ve spent months in Thailand’s capital city. I've visited for weekend girls trips, concerts, and trips with family, staying everywhere from Siam to Chinatown. I've experienced the city's endless ways to fill your days, from world-class museums to addictive street food to some of Asia’s best cocktail bars. If you're planning a stay and want a little more elbow room than the city's hotels might allow, there are plenty of charming rentals to lay your head down at, from studios with incredible river views to massive homes for the whole family to shophouses in Chinatown. Read on for some of the best Airbnbs in Bangkok.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Spacious design, hot tub, screen projector.

Baan Konja sits at the end of a cul-de-sac in the café-crazed neighborhood of Ekkamai. This stylish four-story home is an ideal launching pad for families or groups of friends looking for a peaceful stay. Guests will love how well laid out and spacious the setup is, with elegant tiled bathrooms, a rare private hot tub, four plush bedrooms (three kings and a room with two singles), and a comfy outdoor balcony area. According to past guests, the host, Michael, goes above and beyond to address any issues, including providing toothbrushes and slippers if you forget yours at home. He’s also able to suggest great cocktail spots.

Neighborhood: EkkamaiThings to do nearby: Wat That Thong Buddhist temple; top restaurants, cafés, and bars.

Outfitted with a comfortable bed and couch next to a floor-to-ceiling window, it's designed with local touches like Thai art, colorful throw pillows, and a hand-carved wooden headboard. But travelers are really booking this room for the incredible views over the river and the nearby temple. Just outside, Michelin-star restaurants, riverside cafés, and trendy boutiques are steps away.

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Bangkok?

Recent findings suggest that chinatown and Talat Noi are always my go-to neighborhoods when I'm in Bangkok. They are full of fun, trendy bars, restaurants, and cafés worth spending some time wandering around. Sukhumvit is a great neighborhood for first-timers, with plenty of restaurant options, rooftop bars, and access to the MRT.

When is the best season to visit Bangkok?

Sources indicate that many people suggest that the best time to visit Bangkok is at the end of the rainy season—October through December—before the smog gets bad in January. March to May is the hottest time to visit, so it may be best to avoid if you don't do well in the heat, but I highly recommend planning a trip around Songkran (April 13–15), a.k.a. Thai New Year. It's known for hosting the world's largest water fight, and in my opinion, is one of Asia's best festivals.

#73. Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2 min read (379 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Airlinegeeks

Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Airlinegeeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google parent tech giant Alphabet has agreed to enhanced privacy protections as part of its $10 million bid for data from defunct Spirit Airlines.
  • The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.
  • Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google parent tech giant Alphabet has agreed to enhanced privacy protections as part of its $10 million bid for data from defunct Spirit Airlines.

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.

Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models. The agreement reached this week resolves the unions’ concerns, the Journal remarked.

Google will still get most of the corporate information it originally sought, including millions of emails and Microsoft Teams chats, software code, and data related to revenue, operations, productivity, and other areas. An independent monitor will oversee the tech giant’s handling of the data and ensure privacy and security conditions are being met.

Google and Spirit initially planned to have an outside company “deidentify” the airline’s records. That process will still take place, though at a higher standard than Spirit intended to use, and Google will be prohibited from attempting to “reidentify” the data.

Spirit went out of business in May following a dramatic rise in jet fuel prices. The decision to auction off its internal records for use by AI was a first for the airline industry and opened up a new realm of contestation for workers and employers.

According to recent reports, “Worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a whole upcoming workers’ rights problem,” Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, remarked in a statement. “Without our union, there would have been no one to speak for workers in this fire sale of their private information. We fought and we won brand new protections. Now we will take this issue to all of our employers to secure contractual protections and demand lawmakers protect workers everywhere through federal and state law.”.

#72. A Thief Grabbed His Backpack From A Delta Carousel At JFK, But A Friend Tracked Him Down In Washington, DC

General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

A Thief Grabbed His Backpack From A Delta Carousel At JFK, But A Friend Tracked Him Down In Washington, DC

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A stolen backpack at New York JFK could have been the start of a miserable few weeks for travel writer JT Genter.
  • JT, who writes about points and miles and nomadically travels full-time with his wife Katie, reported that his checked bag had been stolen from Delta’s baggage claim belt at JFK Terminal 4.
  • Checked baggage stolen off of @Delta baggage claim belt in JFK Terminal 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A stolen backpack at New York JFK could have been the start of a miserable few weeks for travel writer JT Genter. Instead, it became an interstate detective story involving a luggage tracker, a bus number, and fellow travel writer Jamie Larounis riding in a Washington, D.C. police car. This one has a happy ending…and Jamie deserves a huge round of applause.

JT, who writes about points and miles and nomadically travels full-time with his wife Katie, reported that his checked bag had been stolen from Delta’s baggage claim belt at JFK Terminal 4. Before leaving the terminal, he filed a missing-baggage claim with Delta and a police report.

Ugh. Checked baggage stolen off of @Delta baggage claim belt in JFK Terminal 4.

Delta missing baggage claim and police report filed before leaving the terminal.

Never had this happen before. Happy for any tips on what to do next.

— JT Genter (@JTGenter) November 11, 2026.

Industry observers note that he subsequently explained that the backpack contained his clothing, medication, toiletries, and irreplaceable mementos. He was also decidedly unimpressed by the response from Delta employees.

Industry observers note that for someone who lives on the road, that is considerably more than losing a suitcase of vacation clothes. Understandably, his bag contains much of his daily life. Replacing the contents becomes another job, and some things cannot simply be purchased again.

But there was something JT had deliberately left out of his initial account.

People understandably suggested that he should have put a tracker inside. In a subsequent upgrade, JT revealed that he already had one. He had kept that information private while police were tracking the man.

And to be precise, this was a Tile tracker, rather than an Apple AirTag.

I appreciate the restraint. When something like this happens, the temptation is to post every development, especially when people are offering advice (and condemnation) about the precaution you already took.

But the more useful audience for those location updates was the people who could actually help recover the bag.

According to Jamie’s account, the man took the stolen backpack from Upcoming York to Washington, DC on Amtrak.

Using the Tile location, Jamie found a man with the bag at a bus station. Then the man boarded a bus.

That could have been the end of the opportunity, but Jamie caught the bus number and found two police officers willing to help. The officers located the suspect a few blocks away and apprehended him.

It has been revealed that they then asked Jamie to ride in the police car to identify the man. Afterward, they went to the station to retrieve the items.

Jamie summed up his unexpected afternoon rather nicely:.

“Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today”.

https://twitter.com/TheForwardCabin/status/2120615885626835334?a=hFcZDL9PoGdHYVjUzks&s=20.

Usually when someone ends up in a police car, the story has taken a less encouraging turn. This was a very welcome exception!

I also love that the bus number became such a useful detail. The tracker got Jamie close enough to spot the bag, but paying attention when the man boarded gave the officers something concrete to work with.

I know Jamie, and I am delighted to see him get credit for this.

In a recent development, there is a considerable difference between feeling sorry for someone who has lost a bag and going out to help find it. Jamie gave his time and followed through when the situation became more complicated than simply spotting a backpack.

The police officers deserve credit too. A location on a tracking app is useful, but recovering stolen property still requires someone to act on that information and I don’t consider it very smart to confront a thief directly. In this case, Jamie found officers who helped turn a promising lead into an actual recovery.

JT’s response to Jamie was understandably enthusiastic:.

He also expressed amazement at how much had been recovered. A great story involving two people I consider friends.

A backpack stolen from a JFK baggage carousel ended up in Washington, where a tracker and a determined friend helped police catch the suspect and recover belongings.

What a satisfying ending. So many missing-bag stories conclude with a claim number and a disappointing reimbursement discussion. This one concluded with Jamie doing some excellent detective work and JT getting back possessions he thought he might never see again.

Industry observers note that well done, Jamie. That is friendship in action!

Good work Jamie. Glad the police gave you a safe assist!

If he’s such an experienced traveler why is he checking his backpack with medication and “momentos?”.

I’m sure the Delta baggage people reminded him of his amateur move which is why he claims that they weren’t helpful.

But, more importantly…why didn’t he post a picture of the thief?

Some of us travel in and out of T4 at JFK and it would be helpful to know who the real garbage is.

Did I miss the part where he says he has a picture of thief? Or do you mean Jamie?

He took and posted pictures of the stolen bag.

It would have been really helpful to have taken a picture of the thief at the same time.

In lieu of that…a nice follow up from him could be a link to the publication of the thief’s official mugshot.

Well, I do have photos of the thief from the JFK security cams and from Jamie’s pursuit. But I’m going to let justice play itself out in the courts, not online.

Mugshots and arrests are public information.

Sources indicate that JT is full time global nomad and does carry several weeks of meds in his carry on. This backpack contains pretty much everything else he travels the world with. This is a little different than a normal vacationer.

“Once again, when the crunch is on, Delta Airlines Staff prove to be absolutely indifferent to the travelers’ plight”.

Just ask the 1.3 million travelers stranded for days during Crowdstrike.

I disagree…the Delta baggage services people gave him some much needed tough love.

Never put medications or “irreplaceable mementos” is checked bags.

The key momento was too large to fit in our carry-on bags, or it would’ve been in there with the others.

As far as medications go, I carry a few weeks’ worth in my carry-on bags. But, since we live on the road and can’t always get an easy refill, I typically have additional meds in my checked bag — along with over-the-counter meds and suppliments.

In a recent development, I had someone steal a brand fresh shirt, still in the plastic bag, from an outside pocket of a checked carryon (yes, it should have been in the case, but it was a last minute purchase). I reported it to Delta and periodically received “we’re looking for your bag” updates. I must have told them 10 times, I have my bag, someone stole a shirt from the bag itself. Finally, they closed the case, saying “sorry, we cannot locate your bag.” I went to the baggage office at my local airport, explained that the item had been stolen from the checked luggage. The agent asked how much it cost and I highlighted her the receipt. She wrote me a check on the spot. Delta’s online baggage claims service is terrible.

Recent findings suggest that how did Jamie have the location? Is that something JT shared with him?

Yes, I was able to share a link with Jamie that had the live-updating Tile tracking information.

#71. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 • ⏱️ 14 min read (2707 words)
General 🌐 Nomadicmatt

Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read | Source: Nomadicmatt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city.
  • Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow.
  • I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you initiative an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Recent findings suggest that this first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

It has been revealed that the route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

Recent findings suggest that after a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

Recent findings suggest that the second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Sources indicate that nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

In a recent development, from here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Sources indicate that madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

According to recent reports, for dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

In a recent development, another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

According to recent reports, the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

Recent findings suggest that the Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial noted to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

In a recent development, to end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

Recent findings suggest that while Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#70. Tech Report: Is It True That The Airbus A321XLR Flies With Its Nose Pitched Up At Cruising Altitude?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Tech Report: Is It True That The Airbus A321XLR Flies With Its Nose Pitched Up At Cruising Altitude?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Did you feel like your plane was a little nose-up on your last long flight?
  • Industry observers note that while a nose-up attitude is basic physics, a couple of factors make it highly noticeable on the A321XLR.
  • Sources indicate that this is not an abnormality of the A321XLR design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Did you feel like your plane was a little nose-up on your last long flight? Well, you're not wrong. In fact, nearly every single commercial jetliner cruises with a noticeable nose-high pitch for most of the journey. The physics of flight dictate that an aircraft on a steady level cruise rarely maintains a perfectly parallel relationship with the horizon. It's especially remarkable on Airbus' newest long-haul narrowbody, the A321XLR.

Industry observers note that while a nose-up attitude is basic physics, a couple of factors make it highly noticeable on the A321XLR. An aircraft wing does not generate lift when aligned perfectly flat with the oncoming air mass. It requires a pitch of two to three degrees above the horizon to force the air under the wings and produce efficient lift. The A321 is a very long narrowbody aircraft, and its silhouette creates a clear visual profile compared to shorter aircraft like the A319.

Sources indicate that this is not an abnormality of the A321XLR design. It is the standard operating condition for the entire commercial fleet, ranging from the small Airbus A220 to the massive Boeing 777. As a flight progresses and the engines burn through fuel, the plane becomes lighter. When it needs less lift, the fly-by-wire system gradually lowers the nose. The cabin floor is rarely level, though the tilt is subtle enough that most passengers won't notice it while seated.

Despite carrying far more weight than other planes in its class, the XLR retains the Airbus A321's baseline wingspan of 117 feet (35.8 meters). Given the restricted wing area compared to a widebody jet that flies similar routes as the XLR, it must fly at a higher angle of attack than many commercial jets. Raising the nose one to two degrees above most other airliners allows the XLR to generate more lift at a similar altitude and airspeed.

It has been revealed that it must take off with a far greater payload than the standard A321neo, which is often configured with a higher seating capacity, because of the fuel it carries to make long journeys. That requires gradual step climbs with the XLR slowly raising and lowering its altitude relative to the fuel in its tanks as the route progresses.

Pilots on simulator forums online cite pitch ranges between one and three degrees for cruise flight. These values fluctuate depending on the precise fuel load, passenger count, and chosen speed schedule. Weight is the primary driver of these fluctuations. For the Airbus A321XLR, this calculation is pushed to the absolute extreme of the single-aisle category. The jet stands out as the heaviest iteration of the A321 family, boasting a maximum takeoff weight reaching 223,000 pounds (101,100 kg).

Recent findings suggest that when heavily loaded with fuel at takeoff, the thin air at high altitudes cannot provide enough density to support an XLR efficiently. To avoid an unfavorable flight profile, the XLR is heavily reliant on step climbs. It will initially level off at a lower altitude where the air is denser. Even at this lower altitude, the engines must operate at high thrust to maintain cruise speed while holding a high nose pitch.

United’s first Airbus A321XLR begins a new premium narrowbody era for long-haul flying.

Sources indicate that walking toward the front of the A321XLR cabin on a transatlantic flight might make a passenger feel as though they are moving up a shallow ramp. While the plane behaves flawlessly from an engineering standpoint, its high nose-up posture changes how passengers experience the flight. That is most noticeable during the initial hours of a transcontinental mission when the aircraft is heaviest.

In a recent development, in the early phase of such a trip, flight attendants must manage heavy galley carts on a tilted floor. Service typically starts from the front of the cabin and moves backward, allowing the crew to push the heavy carts downhill rather than fighting gravity to push them forward. To guarantee a pleasant ride for a full passenger payload, the aircraft relies on a highly optimized, non-emergency 'comfort envelope.'.

To prevent passengers from feeling any sudden jerks or wallowing motions, the autopilot performs continuous micro-trimming. The computers maintain a specific cruise speed, typically Mach 0.78, at an altitude where the air density allows the plane to ride smoothly. By keeping the XLR in the 'buffet margin' performance band, the system ensures a rock-solid, vibration-free ride for the customers in the back.

The story behind Delta's reluctance to invest in long-haul narrowbodies.

Inside the advanced cockpit of the A321XLR, a suite of flight computers handles most of the workload required to balance the jet's pitch. The flight computers eliminate the need for pilots to manually adjust the plane's controls as the trip progresses. These avionics let the flight crew spend more time focused on navigation rather than constantly correcting the aircraft's attitude.

Recent findings suggest that flying at a nose-up angle naturally creates extra aerodynamic drag. To combat this, the computer systems linking the navigation data and the engine throttles work together seamlessly. The autopilot uses a continuous feedback loop that monitors how the aircraft is interacting with the thin air. As the plane burns off fuel and changes mass, the computer automatically commands the tail stabilizers to pivot by microdegrees.

It has been revealed that this smooth, automated adjustment gently lowers the nose to a flatter angle without requiring any input from the flight crew. The system calculates the exact engine thrust needed to glide efficiently at the ideal angle. It maintains a steady cruise speed without burning excess fuel, keeping the plane at the mathematically perfect intersection of pitch, speed, and fuel efficiency.

Analyzing the real world performance of the world's longest range narrowbody.

The A321XLR navigation computer removes all the guesswork from changing altitudes during long-haul flights. The plane cannot safely cruise at its final high altitude right after takeoff because the air is too thin to support it. The automation constantly runs real-time calculations to find the optimal moments to climb. Simultaneously, flying a long-range narrowbody like the XLR near its performance margins also requires strict safety boundaries.

It has been revealed that when the plane reaches an ideal state, the system notifies the crew, executes the climb smoothly, and automatically recalibrates the nose position for the newly introduced altitude. The flight control software also includes hard-coded safety protections that act as an invisible safety net. If severe turbulence or a sudden wind shift tries to force the nose into a dangerously high angle, the computer automatically intervenes. It overrides unsafe tendencies and stabilizes the plane well before it approaches an aerodynamic stall.

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

The automation on the A321XLR acts as both an active stabilizer during rough weather and an immediate backup to the autopilot. The flight computers do not just wait for the plane to get bounced around. Instead, they use a real-time response system. The throttle computer continuously tracks wind shear to detect if a sudden draft causes a drop in speed. Then, the engines instantly spool up to add energy, and if a gust spikes the speed, the throttles dial back.

Recent findings suggest that accelerometers and sensors throughout the fuselage detect sudden pockets of rising or sinking air instantly. By minutely deflecting these wing surfaces in direct opposition to the bumpy air, the plane counteracts the turbulent forces. Even if the autopilot is hand-flying or navigating severe weather, the computer software enforces strict performance limits. If an extreme event exceeds the autopilot's limits, the XLR will drop offline to hand control back to the pilots.

It has been revealed that because an unexpected disconnection is highly critical, the cockpit is designed to make the handover impossible to miss. The plane will not allow the nose to point higher than 30 degrees up or lower than 15 degrees down, and the system limits the maximum roll angle to 67 degrees. If the autopilot projects that intervention is needed to stay within tolerances, red flashing warning lights illuminate directly in front of both pilots on the main dashboard panels.

The evolving industry, and climbing price, of extra-large turbofan engine repairs.

In a recent development, although the A321XLR looks identical to a standard variant of the family, the jet has some subtle differences inside and out to match the flight efficiency of its light, shorter-haul peers. Lighter, standard A321neo jets are optimized for high-capacity, short-haul routes where low-speed lift during frequent takeoffs and landings is a major priority. To achieve this, standard A321s have featured complex, heavy double-slotted inboard flaps. For the A321XLR, Airbus deleted the double-slotted configuration in favor of a single-slotted inboard flap.

The simpler control surface slashes the wing's physical weight and provides an optimized profile that reduces drag in high-altitude cruise. During an 11-hour long-haul cruise, a double-slotted mechanism creates excessive, unnecessary weight and parasitic aerodynamic drag. To ensure the plane doesn't lose low-speed lift during takeoff at maximum weight, Airbus pairs this single-slotted flap with advanced software that introduces automated flap programming.

Looking at the internal components, the XLR once again differs from older long-range models like the A321LR. On the legacy jets, extra fuel is carried in up to three separate additional center tanks which resemble large cargo containers bolted into the luggage hold. These add weight and eat up cargo space that would otherwise be used for bags and shipments. The XLR solves this by replacing separate cargo-bay tanks with a single, permanent rear center tank.

Concentrating thousands of liters of fuel entirely behind the wings completely shifts the aircraft’s weight and balance. As the flight progresses and the aft tank drains, the center of gravity dynamically sweeps forward. The XLR's flight computers use automated fuel management to precisely monitor fuel burn across the outer wings, forward tanks, and rear tank, keeping the plane perfectly balanced in its optimal cruise pitch from takeoff to touchdown.

My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. #68. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words)
General 🌐 Godsavethepoints

What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight.
  • For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about.
  • More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

According to recent reports, even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

It has been revealed that if an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

According to recent reports, as I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

It has been revealed that now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

Industry observers note that that’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

According to recent reports, the major question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#67. Industry News: Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

General 🌐 Airlinegeeks

Industry News: Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read | Source: Airlinegeeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alaska Airlines will bring four upcoming destinations into its domestic network next summer.
  • In a recent development, the carrier confirmed Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle.
  • Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alaska Airlines will bring four upcoming destinations into its domestic network next summer.

In a recent development, the carrier confirmed Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle. Three of the four cities – Jacksonville, Norfolk, and Des Moines – have never had nonstop flights to Seattle.

Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.

The Des Moines service will also mark Alaska’s debut in Iowa.

In a recent development, all four connections will operate daily, year-round. Flights to Charlotte and Norfolk will begin June 10, 2027, with Jacksonville and Des Moines launching later that month, on June 24.

Sources indicate that alaska will also offer seasonal service from Seattle to Guadalajara, Mexico, from March 18, 2027, to Aug. 9. Flights will operate three times weekly, using Boeing 737 aircraft.
