#49. Tech Report: American Airlines Dropped One Bogus Award Fee. Alaska Airlines And Air Canada Keep Collecting Theirs.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words)
General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

Tech Report: American Airlines Dropped One Bogus Award Fee. Alaska Airlines And Air Canada Keep Collecting Theirs.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • American Airlines once charged members $75 to book an award ticket close to departure.
  • On the latest Airlines Confidential podcast, former AAdvantage chief and American Airlines Chief Information Officer Maya Leibman discussed an airline fee she had trouble defending, as flagged by View From The Wing.
  • In a recent development, american continued collecting its close-in award booking fee after the ticketing process became automated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines once charged members $75 to book an award ticket close to departure. The airline eventually eliminated that fee, but a newly introduced account from its former loyalty chief offers a revealing reminder: the work used to justify a charge can disappear long before the charge does.

On the latest Airlines Confidential podcast, former AAdvantage chief and American Airlines Chief Information Officer Maya Leibman discussed an airline fee she had trouble defending, as flagged by View From The Wing.

In a recent development, american continued collecting its close-in award booking fee after the ticketing process became automated. Members without an applicable elite waiver paid $75 when booking within 21 days of departure. Leibman recalled that “we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days,” even though the transaction was “all done automatically.”.

In a recent development, american eliminated the fee in January 2020. Like Gary, I appreciate hearing a former executive acknowledge the tension with collecting money for an expedited process that no longer required anyone to expedite it. I would rather hear that candid admission than a strained argument trying to justify it.

It has been revealed that I can also understand why manually processing an award ticket once required time and resources and understand why an airline might have charged more to complete that work shortly before departure. But when a computer concerns the ticket, what exactly is being expedited?

Recent findings suggest that the airline still has expenses, of course. Maintaining a reservation system costs money. So does operating a loyalty program. But those expenses also exist when someone books a ticket three months before departure and do not explain why an otherwise identical automated transaction should suddenly cost another $75 inside a 21-day window.

The more straightforward explanation is that American could collect the money, so it did.

It has been revealed that airlines do not price everything according to the cost of providing it, and I do not expect them to. A last-minute seat may command a premium because demand supports it. But if that is the rationale, call it a premium for booking at the last minute. Calling it a processing expense just makes frequent flyers jaded. And whatever you call it, customers are understandably going to hate it because it does not correlate to any legitimate expense unless you count the sunk cost of the investment in the automation system.

American dropped its fee, but I see the same problem today with partner award booking fees at Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards and Air Canada Aeroplan.

It has been revealed that I covered the Atmos fee increase earlier this year. Aeroplan also spells out its charge in its flight reward policy and makes it clear when booking online or on the Air Canada app.

These are airline-imposed charges, of course, not government taxes, though they are often lumped into the same section to suggest that you’re paying taxes, not fees. Here, you can do the searching, select the flights, enter your information, and complete an ordinary booking online, yet still pay extra for the privilege of redeeming your points on a partner.

I consider these bogus fees. They are revenue-generating measures, and I will not defend them as some necessary surcharge for the work involved in issuing my ticket. But by bogus that doesn’t mean that I fail to understand why they are levied.

Industry observers note that yes, programs pay partner airlines for award travel, bu that is part of offering partner awards in the first place. It should already inform the economics of selling points and setting redemption prices. Collecting another cash charge from the member is a commercial choice.

For my family of four, the Atmos fee alone adds $160 to a round-trip partner award unless a waiver applies (and I don’t have the credit card right now). That is real money, especially when we are already redeeming a substantial number of points.

There is one concession I will make: these fees are published and displayed during booking. We can account for them when deciding what the points and the program are worth.

If an award costs 50,000 points plus taxes and a partner booking fee, that cash payment belongs in my valuation. I should not calculate the value of the redemption as though the fee does not exist.

A program with an annoying booking fee can still offer a better overall deal than a program without one. I would happily pay $20 to save thousands of points on an otherwise comparable itinerary. But that makes the redemption worthwhile despite the fee. It does not make the fee itself worthwhile.

The same applies when earning or buying points. If I expect to redeem primarily on partners, those charges reduce what I am willing to pay for the currency. Transparency lets us make that calculation, so at least there is that.

American Airlines deserves credit for eventually eliminating its $75 close-in award booking fee. Leibman’s recollection helps explain why members were right to question it: the process became automated, but the charge remained.

Partner award booking fees at Atmos Rewards and Aeroplan strike me as similarly unappealing revenue measures. I still use both programs, and a good redemption can easily outweigh the extra cash required. But I bake those charges into my valuation rather than pretend they are justified by some special service I am receiving.

Sometimes a fee survives because collecting it is profitable, which his hardly breaking news, but something I appreciate Leibman confirming explicitly.

Beond Airlines Suspends Flights Again: Will They Resume In December?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October. Then in October, it unveiled it would return in December. Is that actually happening now, or what exactly is going on?

According to recent reports, beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The manufacturer is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline right now has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Sources indicate that then in October, the airline confirmed that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Interestingly, the airline has promised to provide a schedule update by November 12, 2026, but that date has now come and gone, and there was no update.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of December, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. The company does have a section on its travel updates page with FAQs, and one of the questions is “will the dates change again?” The answer is “we chose dates we are confident in,” but also notes that “if anything changes, you will hear from us first.”.

Sources indicate that beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when looks change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Sources indicate that interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business blueprint was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:.

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:.

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

According to recent reports, as I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in December.

Sources indicate that in the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. That timeline has come and gone, and now the airline claims it’ll resume operations as of December 2026. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

Recent findings suggest that we’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#47. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India.
  • On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.
  • IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a latest strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

Sources indicate that I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a latest manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are massive business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that in a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local manufacturer, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the latest alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following….

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

Sources indicate that in short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its looks. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier intends to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

Recent findings suggest that it will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:.

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

According to recent reports, starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

In a recent development, denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives remarked the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Industry observers note that speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in Upcoming York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

  • Boeing admits the 737 MAX 9 whose door plug blew out on Alaska Airlines flight 1282 “was not reasonably safe in construction” when it left the factory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Boeing admits the 737 MAX 9 whose door plug blew out on Alaska Airlines flight 1282 “was not reasonably safe in construction” when it left the factory. But the planemaker is still fighting to keep passengers from collecting punitive damages. Its argument amounts to tough luck: the airplane was built in Washington, and Washington law generally doesn’t allow those damages. Boeing already won that argument against a mother and her son who was nearly sucked out of the opening in the fuselage. Another group of passengers is trying to show that the misconduct reaches back to decisions made at the company’s former Chicago headquarters – in order to access Illinois law. Boeing has formally acknowledged the defective construction that resulted in the blowout. On January 5, 2024, the Alaska Airlines jet was climbing out of Portland for Ontario, California when the plug departed the airplane at nearly 15,000 feet. The cabin rapidly depressurized. Oxygen masks dropped, belongings flew out, and the pilots brought the aircraft safely back to Portland. Spirit AeroSystems had built the fuselage. At Boeing’s Renton factory, the plug was opened for rivet repairs, then closed without reinstalling the four bolts that kept it from moving. I covered the whistleblower’s account of those missing bolts before investigators eventually confirmed them. The National Transportation Safety Board identified Boeing’s inadequate training, guidance and oversight as the probable cause. “Not reasonably safe in construction” is the language of Washington’s product liability law. A manufacturer can be strictly liable for injuries caused by a product that materially departed from its specifications when it left the manufacturer’s control. That leaves the fight to focus on the value of passenger injuries and whether Boeing can be punished beyond paying compensation. Last month, I wrote about Cynthia Tisher and her son, whose shirt was sucked off his body. According to their lawsuit, his seat pitched toward the opening. His mother held onto him, afraid he’d be pulled out, too. Other passengers helped them move away. Their federal lawsuit sought punitive damages against Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems. The judge ruled that Washington law governed and threw that request out. The blowout happened over Oregon, but the manufacturing failure occurred in Washington. The judge refused to reconsider. The current admission comes in litigation by a 47 plaintiff group suing Boeing, Spirit AeroSystems and Alaska Airlines, which claims Boeing management promised safety improvements to regulators and the public while failing to deliver them. They say decisions at the former Chicago headquarters helped produce the failures that sent this airplane out without its bolts. Boeing’s admission makes sense as litigation strategy. Boeing can argue testimony over how badly it acted is unnecessary to decide how much compensation each passenger deserves. And its strategy turns on getting punitive damages thrown out. #43. Why New Boeing Planes Are Green Before Delivery, But Airbus Aircraft Aren't

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Why New Boeing Planes Are Green Before Delivery, But Airbus Aircraft Aren't

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the observation that pre-delivery Boeing aircraft are green, and Airbus aluminum aircraft aren't, is partially true, but it is far from the full picture.
  • In a recent development, after the peelable Temporary Protective Coating (TPC / "Spraylat") is removed, Boeing aircraft look different, but they are rarely photographed at that stage.
  • Sources indicate that one of the most distinctive features of newly introduced aircraft is the stage they go through when they are in their primary coats of paint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the observation that pre-delivery Boeing aircraft are green, and Airbus aluminum aircraft aren't, is partially true, but it is far from the full picture. There are significant differences in the substances that Boeing and Airbus' various divisions and subcontractors use, and this is partially driven by environmental regulations differing by location. But unfinished Boeing aircraft are also typically photographed at an earlier stage of development compared with Airbus.

In a recent development, after the peelable Temporary Protective Coating (TPC / "Spraylat") is removed, Boeing aircraft look different, but they are rarely photographed at that stage. This is the stage that Airbus aircraft are typically photographed. Importantly, the 'green' conversation requires aluminum aircraft, as composite material structures are treated differently. Here is what to know about Boeing and Airbus coatings.

Sources indicate that one of the most distinctive features of newly introduced aircraft is the stage they go through when they are in their primary coats of paint. Boeing aircraft are green as they roll out of the assembly facility. The green coating is a corrosion-protective primer applied to the aircraft structure before its final exterior paint scheme. The layer also helps subsequent coatings to adhere to the aircraft. Other aircraft manufacturers such as Airbus, Embraer, ATR, and COMAC use broadly comparable surface-protection coatings, although they are not quite the same.

Industry observers note that it is also key to distinguish between the aircraft's three basic stages of coating. Aircraft receive structural primer, intermediate coating, and final decorative topcoats. What looks like a single coat of green paint on Boeing aircraft is actually a combination of two distinct coatings, obviously not the final decorative one. What is seen is typically the Temporary Protective Coating (TPC / "Spraylat") and the Corrosion-Inhibiting Primer (The True Undercoat).

This does not apply to the composite-material-constructed 787 Dreamliner (more on that below). Instead, it is applied to traditional aluminum structures. It is worth noting that while the Boeing 737 is now in its fourth (MAX) generation, its fuselage remains a fundamentally aluminum structure and a 1960s design. Something similar is also true of the heavily updated Boeing 777X soon to enter service. It may come with newly introduced wings, but its fuselage remains primarily aluminum.

Boeing's clean-sheet Boeing 787 is its only 'upcoming' aircraft in the narrow sense of being a clean-sheet design able to take full advantage of today's advanced composite materials. The only 'new' Airbus analog is the Airbus A350. The A330neo and A320neo series are upgraded older aluminum fuselage aircraft. The Boeing 787's fuselage and wings are built with carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) rather than aluminum and so do not suffer from galvanic or atmospheric metal corrosion.

It has been revealed that consequently, Dreamliners do not come with green TPC or green chromate primers. As they roll out of the assembly line, they appear white or light-gray/beige, being coated with conductive/UV-protective primer coats. The Dreamliner's primary competitor, the A350, comes with a tan/beige primer coating, which serves a similar function. Sections in white or beige are usually composite materials, which don't corrode and don't need the coating. That's why the composite-bodied 787 looks less green than the aluminum 737.

Stage 1: component fabrication, sub-assembly transit.

Stage 2: Final assembly, outdoor flight line.

Bare bright silver or matte pale yellow-green.

Industry observers note that this is perhaps the most striking on the Boeing 777X. As stated, it retained the 1990s-era aluminum fuselage. Accordingly, the fuselage is painted green in the signature glossy emerald-green Temporary Protective Coating (TPC). Meanwhile, the wings are made of composite and so receive a white or light-gray UV-protective topcoat that matches the Boeing 787. Boeing has also applied a strippable green film to its early-built 777-9s, which have been stored outdoors awaiting certification for years.

A closer look at the paint and production processes of Boeing airliners.

Airbus' aluminum aircraft are similar, but also different. These receive chromate-free exterior primers, corrosion-protective coatings, and decorative topcoats. But while the basic process is the same, they are still chromate-free. Airbus started introducing chromate-free exterior primers on the A380 in 2016, almost a decade after the Superjumbo entered service. While the Superjumbo was a clean-sheet aircraft, it was not a 'new' aircraft in the sense of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350.

Industry observers note that the A380 was built using the traditional aluminum-alloy fuselage. One of the criticisms of the program was that it was a massive airplane more than it was a new one. Airbus and Boeing operate in different regulatory environments. The European Union has strict REACH chemical regulations that are phasing out hexavalent chromium more aggressively than in the United States.

In 2025, CIRS reported, "the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) unveiled a proposal to restrict the use of carcinogenic hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) substances across the EU. The measure aims to safeguard human health and the environment from the cancer risks associated with these chemicals." This has pushed Airbus to adopt chromate-free primers faster than Boeing. These typically appear tan, beige, or pale yellow. Airbus generally doesn't use Boeing's glossy, peelable emerald green 'Spraylat' transport film. The structural primer is therefore directly visible.

Industry observers note that another distinctive feature of Airbus aircraft is that when assembled, their coatings are a patchwork of shades. Boeing is a national company; Airbus is a multinational company formed from the merger of major European aerospace companies. It has four home countries (the UK, France, Germany, and Spain). Accordingly, it uses a distributed European manufacturing model.

Recent findings suggest that barrels, wings, and tails are fabricated, anodized, and primed at different sites and at different subsidiaries across these countries. Each facility applies its own corrosion-inhibiting primer before they are shipped to be assembled. Those primers have slightly different chemistries, resulting in different shades. When the aircraft is pieced together, it looks like something of a patchwork of mismatched greens, yellows, and tans.

According to recent reports, major contractors include GKN Aerospace (Fokker Aerostructures) in the UK and the Netherlands, Latecoere in France, and Spirit AeroSystems. Airbus radomes are often matte gray or tan (made of composite materials), the nose and forward base are pale yellow-green, the center fuselage is slightly darker olive or lime green, the belly fairing is tan or beige, the wings are light gray over green primer, and the aft is olive green aluminum or tan/gray in composite areas.

The XWB-97's maturity is becoming an advantage over the rival newly introduced GE9X turbofan, helping the program to progress and be perceived as less risky.

In a recent development, unlike Airbus, Boeing uses a peelable green coating to protect the aircraft's aluminum skin. The aluminum skin is relatively thin, and even minor scratches and indentations can require inspection. It protects against environmental damage during manufacturing and transport. Like Airbus, Boeing has components manufactured across a broad geological footprint, and these require transportation.

While Airbus transports many of its components on climate-controlled BelugaXL aircraft (and ferries), Boeing relies on the Open-Air Cross-Country Rail Transit for its core 737 aircraft. Those fuselages are built in Wichita, Kansas, and need to be transported 2,000 miles (3,200 km) by open railcar to Renton and Everett. Boeing's highly modified Boeing 747 Dreamlifters are used for the 787, not normally the 737. The train route is primarily operated by BNSF Railway, with the journey going through Nebraska, Wyoming, Montana, to Washington via Spokane.

Sources indicate that the journey takes around ten to 12 days, with trains taking three to four fuselages at a time (six maximum). In 2018, Aviation Week reported, "In today’s world on the massive airplane you see going down the rail or you see entering the Renton factory the fuselage is already integrated and they are able to start the same day installing the blankets and wiring and going through the production process without having to do any structural work to the airplane.".

Another key factor to consider when comparing Boeing and Airbus during their manufacturing process is that they are typically photographed at different stages of their manufacturing cycle. This creates an apples-to-oranges mismatch. Most familiar photos of green Boeing aircraft show them with the TPC peelable coating, as they are on the railcars or parked at Renton/Everett facilities.

According to recent reports, airbus photos are typically taken when they are being unloaded from a BelugaXL or rolling off the Final Assembly Line. They may be conducting their first customer acceptance flights. This is a later stage than the Boeing aircraft, and they typically sport a raw structural epoxy primer that gives them a flat, chalky, matte finish.

Other factors also explain why Boeing and Airbus aircraft may appear different. Boeing aircraft parked in Washington are frequently pictured in overcast skies, while Airbus aircraft in Toulouse are often in warm Mediterranean sunlight. Even the digital camera may react differently. For example, if a planespotter fills much of the frame with a green fuselage, the camera's Auto White Balance (AWB) may automatically shift the image to magenta and warm tones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A passenger accused of claiming to have a bomb and trying to enter the cockpit of a United Airlines flight had previously been deported twice, then received asylum, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The newly disclosed immigration history adds another troubling layer to an incident that thankfully ended with the aircraft landing safely and the suspect in custody.

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, 34, was arrested after United Airlines flight 2174 from Newark (EWR) to Newly introduced Orleans (MSY) landed on November 9, 2026.

According to recent reports, according the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office, Gomez-Alberto allegedly told cabin crew there was a bomb onboard. DHS separately alleges an attempt to enter the cockpit. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted:.

“This criminal illegal alien attempted to storm the cockpit, hijack a plane and claimed he had a bomb. Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars. This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system.”.

He went on to claim Gomez-Alberto was a “fraudster” trying to scam his way into the USA, but President Trump is cracking down.

The Boeing 737 MAX 9 carried 46 passengers and six crew members. Deputies arrested Gomez-Alberto after arrival, with local booking charges including communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing. The FAA confirms that the flight landed safely around 11:10 pm following a passenger disturbance and claims it will investigate.

The immigration history has attracted considerable attention, and understandably so.

Industry observers note that according to DHS, Gomez-Alberto was apprehended after entering the United States illegally in 2011 and again in 2014, and removed following both encounters. A third encounter with Border Patrol occurred near San Ysidro, California, in 2019.

An immigration judge ordered release from custody pending removal proceedings in January 2020. DHS now says an immigration judge subsequently granted asylum. The asylum claim cited fear of persecution for being transgender.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has lodged a detainer with the local sheriff’s office, which is a a legal notice or hold placed on an individual or property to prevent their release or transfer.

It has been revealed that two deportations followed by another entry and an eventual asylum grant certainly warrant a closer look at the record. What information did the government have? What did the judge consider? Were there warning signs relevant to public safety? Was there anything more than this?

But the reported asylum grant is also an vital part of that record. Describing the earlier illegal entries does not, by itself, establish the person’s immigration status at the time of this flight, not that I am trying to defend him here.

DHS has accused Gomez-Alberto of exploiting the asylum system. That may well be the case, but the subsequent alleged conduct aboard an airplane does not establish that the original persecution claim was fabricated…we have not seen the full immigration decision or the evidence considered.

Thus, we need those answers before declaring exactly where the system failed.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, imagine being aboard that flight. A claimed bomb and an alleged attempt to reach the pilots are about as frightening as an onboard disturbance gets.

Recent findings suggest that I am thankful this flight reached Latest Orleans safely and that law enforcement took the suspect into custody. Whatever the eventual criminal findings or immigration consequences, the allegations concern conduct that could have endangered everyone onboard.

Recent findings suggest that there is no basis here to conclude that United should have refused transportation simply because of his asylum history. If authorities had information that should have prevented boarding, that would be a separate and very important question….

I expect this to be counterproductively politicized, but I also think this person is very sick to engage in such an act.

It has been revealed that A United Airlines passenger faces criminal charges following an alleged bomb threat and attempted cockpit intrusion. DHS now says the suspect had been deported twice before receiving asylum based on a claim of feared persecution for being transgender.

That history deserves scrutiny, including a clear account of what officials knew and when. But at least he is in custody and I am grateful the aircraft landed safely and this frightening incident ended without a successful cockpit breach.

This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded.

  • As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

It has been revealed that in the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

Recent findings suggest that but now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

According to recent reports, and the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

Recent findings suggest that the trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

According to recent reports, as an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Number of guests: 20+Bed and bath: 9 bedrooms, 8.5 bathsWhy we love it: Gazebo, valley views, fireplace.

Located in the heart of Ohio’s Amish country, Hillside Villa is a bucolic escape for the extended family. While the entire villa can be booked (check for availability on the “Premier House” option), you can also opt for individual units, from a deluxe room for two with a jetted hot tub to a junior room that sleeps up to four. Each comes with scenic views of the hills, along with shared kitchen access (coffee and tea maker provided). There are 55-inch flat-screen TVs too, along with features like fireplaces and porches. In the backyard, you’ll find a gazebo with a firepit, perfect for watching the sunset descend over the farm-filled valley.

Location: Millersburg, OhioThings to do nearby: Country Acres Mini Golf, Pro Football Hall of Fame, Belden Village Mall.

Number of guests: 14Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Contemporary interior design, private lake access, barbecue.

Offering 200 feet of private lakefront in Austin, this modern four-bedroom is a rare retreat. Ideal for a multigenerational family, it’s composed of a main house with two king bedrooms and a guesthouse with a king bedroom, plus a large bunk room with eight twin beds. Spend your days gliding along the lake on a kayak or paddleboard, floating on the 16-foot lily pad, or taking a hike through the surrounding Balcones Canyonland Preserve. End the fun on the two-story party dock, where you can enjoy a meal outside, with s’mores for dessert around the firepit.

Location: Austin, TexasThings to do nearby: Lake Austin, Sixth Street, University of Texas at Austin.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hiking trail access, pool table, forest views.

Recent findings suggest that this Yosemite home, with its breathtaking cathedral windows and stone fireplace, will offer the family a stay they won’t forget. The perfect place to retreat to after a day spent at Yosemite National Park, this four-bedroom is wonderfully western, with its hanging deer antlers, wooden furniture, and tons of colorful textiles. Your group can spread out between two queen beds, two twin beds, and two bunk beds (one with a trundle). Prepare meals in the fully equipped kitchen, then enjoy some family time at the dining table, which seats up to 10. Up in the loft, you’ll find a mini arcade, a number of board games, and a pool table.

Location: Yosemite National Park, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Yosemite National Park, Yosemite Valley, Yosemite Arch Rock Gate Entrance.

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Mountain views, gym, wildlife sightings.

Industry observers note that cozy, inviting, and lived-in, this Jackson Hole property is the ultimate mountain escape. Located in Spring Creek Ranch, the home is in a 1,000-acre ranch community, perched atop East Gros Ventre Butte, 800 feet above the valley floor. The first thing you’ll notice upon walking in is a kitchen and dining area that flows into the living room, with large windows overlooking the mountains. There are four bedrooms (three kings and one with two twin beds), each with views of the Tetons. Poke around the woods, watch a movie around the fireplace, and look out for elk.

Location: Jackson, WyomingThings to do nearby: Jackson Hole Valley, Jackson Hole Wildlife Safaris, Jackson Town Square.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Scenic views, in-unit washer/dryer, beach access.

In Quebec City, the Saguenay Fjord stretches over 62 miles and is surrounded by dramatic granite cliffs. This charming, four-bedroom home will place you right in front of the action. Settle back on the front porch with your loved ones and watch the tides roll in, or take sunset walks along the beach. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need for meals at home, while the grand dining table looks out into the water. Outside, there’s a swing for little ones, plus a few Adirondack chairs for the adults to continue savoring the view.

Location: Saguenay, Quebec City, CanadaThings to do nearby: Saguenay River, Theatre du Palais Municipal, Okwari Le Fjord.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathroomsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, chef available upon request, beach access.

Industry observers note that dreaming of a family reunion across the border? At this bungalow in Placencia, Belize, you’ll have the Caribbean Sea right at your doorstep. Ideal for two families, the four bedrooms (one king and three queens) are spread out in such a way that two of them have their own separate entrance. Spend your days soaking up the sun, swimming in the saltwater pool, gliding along the water on a stand-up paddleboard, or preparing a fresh lunch in the outdoor kitchen. And if you truly want to leave your worries at the door, in-house chef services are available upon request.

Location: Placencia, MexicoThings to do nearby: Placencia Beach, Placencia Pier, Maya Beach.

Number of guests: 18Bed and bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathsWhy we love it: Panoramic windows, hot tub, in-unit washer/dryer.

For extra-large families with great taste, this eight-bedroom beach house is a no-brainer, with jaw-dropping, panoramic views of Lake Michigan and plenty of luxe amenities, from a hot tub and game room to a heated pool. There are gorgeous design details throughout, like vaulted wooden ceilings and circular ship-style windows. Rooms are split between the main house and guest house, with two separate kitchens. Just an 11-minute walk from Saugatuck Dunes State Park, the house provides access to endless scenic trails. Bonus: It’s pet-friendly too.

Location: Saugatuck, MichiganThings to do nearby: Kalamazoo River, Saugatuck Dunes State Park, Oval Beach.

Photo Caption: A render of Four Seasons Resort and Residences Amaala at Triple Bay.

Saudi hotel developers are still building through Houthi attacks, and a record pipeline reveals it. But their bet rests on domestic and religious travel. The international guests that Vision 2030 needs are the ones the attacks are scaring off.

A month after a Houthi missile killed 13 people at Riyadh’s main airport, Saudi Arabia’s hotel pipeline is at a record. Developers and operators say they know of no projects canceled because of the attacks. What the attacks have damaged is harder to rebuild: the kingdom’s image as a safe place to visit.

The attacks have closed airports, canceled the kingdom’s biggest events and pushed up the cost of insuring against conflict. Investors are still signing deals, betting that domestic and religious travel will carry the market until the fighting stops. How long that takes is an open question.

It has been revealed that saudi Arabia’s hotel pipeline has kept growing. The kingdom has a record 401 projects in development, up 15% from a year ago, according to Lodging Econometrics. Those projects will collectively add 109,320 rooms, a 16% increase. That is 52% of the Middle East’s total project count, and 58% of its rooms.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

According to recent reports, A month after a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, Saudi Arabia's hotel pipeline is at a record 401 projects and 109,320 rooms, up 15% and 16% respectively from a year ago, according to Lodging Econometrics. Developers and operators told Skift they know of no projects canceled because of the attacks, though IHG CEO Elie Maalouf remarked some would probably be delayed. The damage is showing up elsewhere: 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between October 8 and late October, according to Cirium data; the Saudi Grand Prix, the Future Investment Initiative, and the Red Sea International Film Festival were scrapped, postponed, or moved; and the U.S. Embassy now requires government employees to get special authorization to use any Saudi airport. This year's openings are concentrated on the Red Sea coast — Four Seasons, Rosewood, Six Senses, Equinox, Nammos, and Raffles — the properties most dependent on the international guests the attacks are deterring. Investors are leaning on a domestic base that accounted for 93.3 million tourists in 2025, or 76.1% of the total, plus religious travel for Hajj and Umrah. Growth had already stalled before October, with 61.2 million tourists in the first half of 2026, up about 1% year over year, against a Vision 2030 target of 150 million a year.

#37. American Airlines Tells Flight Attendants To “Speak Up”—So Nearby Passengers Hear The Credit Card Pitch

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23 min read (4579 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

American Airlines Tells Flight Attendants To “Speak Up”—So Nearby Passengers Hear The Credit Card Pitch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that american Airlines is teaching flight attendants to answer credit card questions loudly enough that nearby passengers hear the pitch, and to use stories about family, friends and other cardmembers to sell the benefits.
  • Recent findings suggest that A slide from recent flight attendant sales training lays out six tips.
  • The slide presents these as best practices from fellow flight attendants:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that american Airlines is teaching flight attendants to answer credit card questions loudly enough that nearby passengers hear the pitch, and to use stories about family, friends and other cardmembers to sell the benefits. A slide from recent flight attendant sales training lays out six tips. The most revealing one is “Speak up.” When one passenger asks about the card, American wants the answer to attract the attention of everyone around them. You may have declined the brochure, but the next row’s question is another chance to sell you. The slide presents these as best practices from fellow flight attendants: Share specific examples or stories. Use anecdotes from cardmembers, family or friends to explain how the card can help. Know your facts. Review the brochure and become comfortable discussing the benefits. Speak up. Answer questions at a volume that lets neighboring passengers hear. The slide notes projecting your voice will attract their interest and curiosity. Take initiative. Coordinate with the other flight attendants about who makes the announcement and who walks the aisle. The cabin lights must remain on. Consider the timing of the flight and avoid making the announcement when the lights are off. Treat customer information confidentially. Never share, copy, photograph or retain personal information encountered on an application or screen. Knowing the product and protecting personal information are basic requirements. Coordinating the crew’s efforts means one announcement and brochures for passengers who want them. The stories, volume and lights are where this gets interesting. American Has More Riding On Its Citi Partnership Onboard credit card sales have been around for years. Under American’s old arrangement, Barclays had the inflight acquisition channel while Citi had other ways to acquire customers. The expanded Citi agreement brings those channels together under an exclusive U.S. card issuer. I’ve reported that the new relationship has been described to me as a joint venture. American’s stake goes beyond supplying miles and benefits to a bank. They’re more closely tied to the performance of the card business itself. A bank collects interchange, annual fees and interest, and pays for funding, credit losses, rewards and acquiring customers. Sharing in the economics of that business gives American more reason to care about who applies, who keeps the card, and who actually uses it. Getting another application on a flight is the beginning of that relationship. American also needs passengers to like the airline enough to keep it in their wallets. The sales push has been building. In May, I covered top inflight card sellers receiving a Clearwater, Florida getaway. Card approvals have also become accelerators in American’s flight attendant performance scoring. In August, I wrote about the push to get flight attendants more excited about selling. American was emphasizing both how much crew could earn and how providing better service would make passengers more receptive. The airline has a good audience for its card: people already buying its flights. Scott Kirby brought onboard pitches to United, which made them mandatory in 2018. These pitches work. Whether making them longer, louder or more frequent works well enough to justify annoying everyone else is a different calculation. Flight Attendants Object To Being Required To Train For Voluntary Sales On October 15, the Association of Professional Flight Attendants objected to American putting a 15-minute card sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. According to the union, management first tried to include it in third quarter training, backed off after objections, then inserted it in the fourth quarter package. Completing the module qualifies flight attendants for the program and makes them eligible for a $25 qualification reward. Selling remains voluntary. The union’s objection is that employees who haven’t chosen to sell are being required to take the sales training anyway, and that required training should focus on safety, security and performing their jobs. Some flight attendants welcome commissions on approved applications. Others resent being drawn into selling financial products. Read The Script, Tell Stories, And Make Sure Other Rows Hear American’s announcement guidance requires the approved script to be read verbatim. It should take about a minute and be delivered once per flight segment. That’s in tension with telling flight attendants to share cardmember stories. Adding an anecdote to the announcement would depart from the script. And then there’s the direction to speak loudly enough that neighboring passengers hear. An individual conversation becomes an unscripted sales pitch to several rows. I’ve criticized onboard claims about bonuses covering two roundtrips to Hawaii when that wasn’t generally realistic. “Know your facts” is good advice. But familiarity with a brochure doesn’t necessarily equip someone to explain award availability or the restrictions on a benefit. Encouraging personal stories, delivered so that other passengers overhear, brings regulatory risk into the sales process. Lights On Shouldn’t Become A Reason To Keep Passengers Awake The slide says, “The cabin lights must remain on,” followed by an instruction to consider flight timing and avoid announcements when the lights are off. Read together, that means choosing an already illuminated part of the flight. It doesn’t tell flight attendants to turn on the lights and wake everyone for a pitch. American’s separate guidance says to make the announcement at cruise, before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. It excludes late night and redeye flights and tells crew to refrain during delays, diversions and other disruptions. Having the lights on doesn’t erase those restrictions. I covered similar limits in 2019, when American told me they were existing training rather than new rules. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary ».

Industry observers note that one of the most annoying moments on a flight is the credit card pitch over the loudspeaker, being forced to hear the 1,000th monotonous message. The airplane environment is already stressful enough from noise and crowding. It even pieces through my noise-canceling headphones.

Industry observers note that crews should not have to do this. They don’t want to. We, the passengers, don’t want them to. This is just management and banks forcing unnecessary things on all of us. Block spam.

This is just another reason I hate unions.

According to recent reports, the last American flight I took was later October out of Phoenix. I don’t remember where the crew was based, but we were not subjected to the credit card spiel. I was going to thank them when disembarking but then thought that could cause problems for them. The lack of the sales push was enjoyable.

They don’t “have” to do it. Numerous other jobs don’t have this requirement. Enhancement that resume.

To strengthen branding and passenger participation for the Citi®/AAdvantage® Executive card, I recommend putting the American Airlines and Citi logos on every sheet of aircraft lavatory toilet paper. Because nothing notes “premium travel experience” quite like a captive audience using premium two-ply corporate messaging.

Industry observers note that of course crews should have to do this. The credit cards are the profit center of the airlines. You can’t complain about things like AA’s profitability on the one hand and then not play a role in pitching the profit center on the other.

And – spoiler alert – this is why having screens at every seat is essential. You can put your phone down for 30-60 seconds when the wifi ads play. But screens that cannot be turned off that are directly in front of your face….

What you really want is a 45 second celebrity video pitching the card first, and then the FAs come back over the loudspeaker with the current offer and then walk down the aisle smiling with the applications.

Industry observers note that and gamify it! Everyone can apply while they are in flight with free wifi. First one on the plane that applies gets an extra 10k miles on top of the already generous SUB. Second person gets an extra 5k. Something like that.

It’s only a matter of time before FAs that sell the most get to jump up the seniority ladder. I’d be pushing for that hard if I was negotiating the next union contract on the airline side.

#36. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11 min read (2219 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status.
  • Recent findings suggest that the reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines.
  • In a recent development, on the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

Recent findings suggest that the reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

In a recent development, on the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

Recent findings suggest that one way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

Industry observers note that we don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Industry observers note that keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

Sources indicate that you can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

It has been revealed that for avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉.

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:.

According to recent reports, assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

According to recent reports, american even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:.

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

According to recent reports, in 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a tech giant to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

Industry observers note that so I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

Sources indicate that the “major three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:.

Recent findings suggest that concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree….

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

The automatic domestic upgrades were nice, the Flagship Lounge access impressed friends and family (said one experienced traveler when we were handed champagne at the FL in ORD, "Wow, I heard stories about this but assumed it was an urban legend"), the expediters at certain international airports were helpful, and getting to the front of the lines during storms and chaotic days like today was reassuring. The most key benefit, though, was the elimination of hassles -- the tight connection, the missed flight and, in one memorable case, helping my daughter get out of Paris in the midst of a nationwide transportation strike when she wasn't even flying AA. When I left for a upcoming position at a much smaller firm, I was able to keep my CK status for the remainder of the program year (about six months). Watching it flip to "Executive Platinum" at 12:01 am on March 1 -- yes, I stayed up to mourn -- was unnerving, but somehow I survived...

Sources indicate that as AA evolved over the years, it wasn't a fit for me any longer. At the same time, I recognized there was an opportunity cost to sticking with AA. And, I found I could secure most of the CK benefits I received for substantially less than that opportunity cost.

Industry observers note that hotel restaurants are becoming destinations again. The smartest owners are giving chefs and operators the freedom to create places with their own character and following, rather than trying to serve every guest at every hour.

When César Ritz and Auguste Escoffier took over the Savoy hotel in London around 1890, they made its dining room the place to be seen. High-society women rarely ate in public then, but Ritz set out to make it irresistible. He fussed over lampshades until the light turned a flattering apricot, hired an orchestra for weekend nights, and insisted on evening dress.

On the food front, Escoffier supplied the reasons to come back, creating Peach Melba for Nellie Melba and getting frogs' legs past the Prince of Wales by calling them nymphs' thighs.

In a recent development, newly introduced money soon rubbed elbows with dukes, actors and the occasional prince. For eight years, the dining room was the reason the hotel stood out. Success went to their heads. The Savoy fired them in 1898 over missing wine and supplier kickbacks, with its owner, Richard D'Oyly Carte, complaining that they had "forgot they were servants.".

Three months later they opened the Hôtel Ritz in Paris, and the man's name.

Hotel restaurants are being rebuilt as destinations with their own identity rather than all-purpose outlets serving every guest need. The article traces the idea to César Ritz and Auguste Escoffier at the Savoy in the 1890s, when the dining room was the reason the hotel stood out, and argues that hotel kitchens later became Swiss Army knife utilities covering early breakfast, business lunch, late dinner, and midnight room service — a menu written to offend nobody. The current shift separates the headline restaurant from daily guest feeding: Baldi at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills serves neither breakfast nor lunch, NUNA at the Four Seasons Miami focuses on dinner while Edge handles breakfast and lunch, and Kwame Onwuachi's Dōgon at the Salamander in Washington operates five evenings a week. Owners are also choosing operators with existing local followings over celebrity-chef prestige alone — the Waldorf replaced Jean-Georges's first West Coast restaurant with a local restaurant dynasty. The payoff, per the article, is social gravity: repeat local visits, cultural relevance, and business value that has little to do with occupancy upstairs. The cost is giving restaurateurs freedom to operate on their own terms.

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

In a recent development, “Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate statement, the FAA said a communications glitch affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights at the moment in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin mentioned there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin stated it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

In a recent development, it was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.
