#31. Breaking: Airbus' Clever Engineering Tricks That Made The A330 Become The "Butter Machine"

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Breaking: Airbus' Clever Engineering Tricks That Made The A330 Become The "Butter Machine"

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Airbus A330 has earned an unusual nickname among aviation enthusiasts: the “Butter Machine.” The name comes from its reputation for exceptionally smooth landings, often marked by a gentle first contact between the rear wheels and the runway before the rest of the landing gear settles.
  • In a recent development, so what exactly is Airbus doing under the wings?
  • Recent findings suggest that the first clue is the tilt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Airbus A330 has earned an unusual nickname among aviation enthusiasts: the “Butter Machine.” The name comes from its reputation for exceptionally smooth landings, often marked by a gentle first contact between the rear wheels and the runway before the rest of the landing gear settles.

In a recent development, so what exactly is Airbus doing under the wings? Which parts are true engineering tricks, and which are folk wisdom repeated on aviation forums for twenty years? Even the experts disagree about why the gear sits at an angle, and the answer changes how you should read every “smoothest landing ever” video. Stay with us, because the most surprising answer sits in the middle of the article, and it comes from pilots who say the landings that look smoothest from the fence are not always the ones passengers feel as smooth. Let’s start with the part everyone can see.

Recent findings suggest that the first clue is the tilt. According to Flightradar24, the A330 is often called ‘The Butter Machine’ because of its smooth landings, and it names the main landing gear as the jet’s easiest identifier: two sets of four wheels, tilted backward. Canada’s Transportation Safety Board (TSB) describes the same arrangement in an A330 investigation report: each bogie carries four wheels in a twin-tandem layout, and the bogies are inclined so the rear tires touch the runway first. Flightradar24 adds a useful contrast: the four-engine A340 carries an extra center landing gear, while the A330 relies on its two main bogies alone, which puts even more attention on how those two units behave.

According to recent reports, that arrangement becomes more interesting once the wheels actually meet the runway. According to the same report, forces are transferred gradually when the wheels touch down, instead of arriving through all eight main tires at once. Simple Flying’s explainer on why the A330 lands so smoothly adds the supporting cast: oleo-pneumatic shock absorbers, a balanced bogie design, titanium and corrosion-resistant steel, and two landing gear control units that alternate for reliability.

The wheels, however, cannot simply remain tilted on their own. Something has to position the bogie before touchdown and control its movement as the aircraft transitions from flight to the runway.

Industry observers note that that job belongs to a hydraulic ram called a pitch trimmer. Pilots and engineers on the PPRuNe forum describe it as the part that sets the bogie nose-up when the gear is selected down, and a research paper on tire heat at touchdown says it lifts the front wheels of the bogie and lets the rear wheels descend around the bogie beam. The same paper adds that the pitch trimmer can act like a shock absorber.

That damping role is not just forum talk. A patent for a variable-damping pitch trimmer explains that the actuator positions the wheels before touchdown, helps stow the gear, and also damps the motion of the bogie beam relative to the leg. Meanwhile, a shortening mechanism pulls the shock absorber up inside the leg during retraction, which shrinks the gear so it fits into a compact bay. Simple Flying notes that Airbus had not used such a feature on many earlier models. The TSB report adds that the bogie beam pivots at its center on the shock strut, and that the beam position is always the same when the gear is selected.

That last point is vital because it separates two jobs that are often blended together when the A330’s landing gear is discussed. The pitch trimmer clearly helps position and damp the bogie, while the shortening mechanism helps package the landing gear inside the aircraft. That raises a bigger question about the original purpose of the backward tilt itself.

Delta is right now the world's largest A330-900 operator, while Cathay Pacific has the most on order.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for the angle is less settled than the nickname might suggest. In a PPRuNe thread on landing gear lean, a contributor insists that simple geometry points to storage, noting that the tilt exists so the bogie fits the bay. Another poster counters that the A330 and A340 are a special case, claiming the nose-up tilt is intentional and works a bit like the semi-levered gear on the Boeing 777-300ER, improving clearance under the aft fuselage.

Recent findings suggest that enthusiasts keep a dedicated Airliners.net thread on A330 main gear bogie tilt, while The Points Guy reports that wheel orientation is mostly a space-saving choice, even though pilots generally agree that trailing-link gear produces the most flattering landings. In other words, the tilt may exist for storage, yet it still shapes the touchdown. Designers rarely mind when a packaging solution doubles as a comfort feature.

According to recent reports, the landing gear explains why the A330 touches down in stages, but it does not explain everything passengers see or feel during the final seconds of a landing. Once the aircraft is close to the runway, the flight-control system and the wing become just as important.

The A330 was designed to give pilots familiar handling near the runway even though it uses fly-by-wire controls. According to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ASB), flare mode replaces the normal load-factor law with a flare law, letting crews use the same landing technique as on non-fly-by-wire aircraft. Airbus’ own Safety First magazine indicates the flare should begin around 40 feet (12 meters) above the runway on the A330, A340, A350 and A380, compared with 30 feet (nine meters) on smaller Airbus jets. The same article warns that a steeper approach slope than the nominal three degrees may call for an earlier flare, reminding pilots that the software supports them rather than replacing their timing.

In a recent development, handling plays a part too. Many pilots describe the A330 as stable and predictable, with an older-generation wing that gives a slightly heavier control feel than the A350. Members of the Infinite Flight Community go further, crediting a wing size and strong ground effect, though that is speculation rather than confirmed engineering. A pilot on a PPRuNe flare-height thread offers a more practical view, saying the A330 and A340 settle nicely with a 40-foot (12-meter) retard and a smooth rotation.

With the gear tilted, the bogie damped, and the flare law handling the final phase, the ingredients for a smooth touchdown are certainly there. There is still one catch, though: the first contact with the runway is not necessarily the end of the landing sensation.

From mass to mechanics: why the A380 needs more wheels than a semi-truck.

It has been revealed that on a PPRuNe thread about hard A330 landings, pilots describe how the aircraft can touch down beautifully on the rear wheels, then float along the runway before the front wheels come down heavily. Their advice is to touch down on the rear wheels, then pitch down firmly enough to bring the front wheels gently onto the runway while speed remains, which is exactly what they say the autopilot does on an autoland. That distinction changes how the A330's landing should be judged from the ground. A long, graceful hold-off can look almost perfect to somebody watching from the fence while producing a noticeably firmer second contact for people inside the aircraft. The sequence is therefore less about eliminating every bump than about controlling when each part of the landing gear takes the load.

It has been revealed that timing matters for another reason. A separate thread about A340 touchdowns explains that applying reverse thrust as the rear axle lands can make the aircraft drop onto the front axle once the ground spoilers kill the lift, and that a higher pitch attitude at the flare makes the thump worse. A pilot in the same thread claims the A330 behaves similarly, and that the cure is to flare for the rear axle, derotate smoothly until the front axle is down, and only then use reverse. Ground spoiler logic, according to an ATSB investigation of an A330 landing, depends on weight on both main gears plus either a radio altitude below 6 feet (1.8 meters) or a wheel speed above 72 knots (133 kilometers per hour). One Airliners.net user also lists three distinct bumps: rear wheels, front wheels, then the nose wheel.

The sequence also explains why the A330's landing gear remains interesting beyond the aircraft itself. Airbus did not stop developing large-aircraft landing gear after the A330, and some of the same principles appear on later widebodies.

The A330's basic approach clearly survived into later Airbus designs. As Simple Flying previously explored, the A350-1000’s six-wheel bogie is built, so the rear wheels typically touch down first, stabilizing the aircraft before the forward wheels settle, which reduces pitching forces and improves comfort. The A380 needs 20 tires on its main gear, which demonstrates how far the same weight-spreading problem can be pushed. Both aircraft inherit the same basic logic: share the load, sequence the contact, and let the shock absorbers do the rest.

Airbus also launched the A330neo with new engines and winglets that improved per-seat fuel economy by 14 percent, but the family's touchdown personality barely figures in that story.

That is what makes the landing gear such an interesting part of the A330's legacy. The aircraft has evolved through new engines and winglets, but the gear that helped create the Butter Machine reputation remains fundamentally part of the family. As the NEO version continues to fly across more route networks, pilots, passengers, and spotters still get the same butter landings.

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

It has been revealed that cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

It has been revealed that I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Industry observers note that the route originally released in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

In a recent development, it was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun upcoming ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

Industry observers note that the Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

According to recent reports, it was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

Recent findings suggest that I chose seat 18K. These seats are 20.5 inches wide with plenty of pitch. There are no sliding doors, but there is a privacy wing at level with a passenger's face.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are presently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.).

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

According to recent reports, not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

Industry observers note that I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced latest service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Industry observers note that award search tools are increasingly a major part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

In a recent development, flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Recent findings suggest that business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly rolled out (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

An airline credit card can save you enough in checked bag fees to justify keeping it, but cost you hundreds of dollars in rewards if you use it for your spending.

It has been revealed that in this week’s episode of Airlines Confidential, Ed Pizzarello favored flexible bank points while former American AAdvantage President Maya Leibman preferred the simplicity of airline and hotel cards. Later, she recalled something an unnamed former loyalty program president had told her:.

“people will pay anything for a free flight.”.

In a recent development, for at least the last decade and a half I’ve been arguing that getting an airline card for benefits doesn’t mean it should become your default payment method, and that there are different distinct reasons to get a card besides payment processing (and bundled financing): An initial bonus. Spending enough to earn a large bonus can make sense even when the card’s normal earning rate isn’t attractive. And the bonus can be a reason to apply for the card, but you still need to decide if it’s worth using for ongoing spend. Benefits that come with keeping it. Checked bags, boarding benefits, lounge access or an anniversary certificate can justify the annual fee. The card may belong in the sock drawer, not your wallet, if actual rewards for spend aren’t great enough. Rewards for actual spending. This is where the return on the next dollar matters, including any status credit or spending threshold you’re working towards. Some benefits require paying with the card. Make the purchases needed to use those benefits. That still doesn’t make the card the best choice for the rest of your spending. Holding a UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) is great if you fly United because you earn more miles, and then you spend fewer miles on your redemptions. That doesn’t require spending on the card itself. What Your Free Flight Actually Costs Put $30,000 of spending on a card earning one airline mile per dollar, and you earn 30,000 miles. #27. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there.
  • But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense.
  • In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to newly introduced applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:.

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:.

Industry observers note that IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:.

In a recent development, marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:.

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

Sources indicate that I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples….

Recent findings suggest that I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a significant purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including substantial welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

Recent findings suggest that the best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#26. Industry News: My First “Latest” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

📅 01 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words)
General 🌐 Godsavethepoints

Industry News: My First “Latest” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

📅 01 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card.
  • The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards.
  • Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

According to recent reports, chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Sources indicate that which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a upcoming “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

According to recent reports, previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the upcoming version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in Upcoming York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Recent findings suggest that typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

In a recent development, if I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

Industry observers note that BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive….

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

It has been revealed that if Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

According to recent reports, you can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Personally, I sit down on it, eat the food, sleep and arrive somewhere I need to be. It’s a tiny cocoon of transport. Not a hotel room. Yes, I want comfort and decent things to pass the time. But anyone who obsesses over feeling less comfortable given a yellow stripe needs to seriously assess priorities.”.

In a recent development, I understand that sentiment and agree that the comfort and quality of the seat, bedding, food, and drinks is far more key the color of the seat. Even so, the issue is that Singapore Airlines prides itself on the small details and the current mockup looks like a sloppy and callous oversight.

In a recent development, that’s certainly a matter of opinion, but what strikes me is that “the internet” has had a field day creating alternate design schemes. Look at this collage of alternatives, for examples:.

A post shared by Dennis Chong (@dennischongofficial).

According to recent reports, every one of those strikes me as preferable to the chosen design and some look downright luxe and in the rich tradition of Singapore Airlines. This one is my favorite:.

People are joking about what’s next, wondering if we might soon see fresh flight attendant uniforms to replace the sarong kebaya?

(Ironically, these looks like Starlux uniforms, which BMW/Designworks also designed).

Recent findings suggest that I’ll leave it here, but I’d still really like to know the thought process that drove this seat design. Who agreed that this was a great fresh design, especially when it truly looks like Scoot, your low-cost subsidiary?

I’m still betting that SIA is going to scrap the black/yellow design and come up with something upcoming, but that’s about as theoretical at this point as the “new uniforms” above.

Join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Sources indicate that matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Is this the most important thing in life? Obviously not. Has no impact on my life.

It has been revealed that but it’s just a complete and abject failure of maintaining a luxury brand. A case study in stupidity. And sorry folks, branding matters.

In a recent development, the shame of it is that what looks like a beautiful new first class design has basically been completely ignored in favor of commenting on this spectacular failure. “Here’s our new profit center – great news, we made it look cheap and bland and just like our low cost airline” is the sentiment that is being put forward. That’s unbelievable!

In a recent development, this wasn’t a complicated assignment. The fact that they bungled it so badly is incredible. Someone at the airline will surely be held accountable for this, whether the internet thinks that’s fair or not.

Given that BMWs are the most super-mega-fugly vehicles on the road, it’s no surprise that this design is a total flop. That said, the mystery of why SQ management signed-off on it does still remain.

In a recent development, what in the world is the basis of the newly introduced yellow stripe and gray design? Is it some type of “ode to Spirit Airlines”? Certainly not aligned with a premium product. Singapore Airlines was a special experience. It’s going to be difficult to watch Singapore Airlines’ Bud Light moment.

#24. The Moment I Saw This Gorgeous Lake Como Airbnb, I Knew I Had to Strategy a Trip to Perledo

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

The Moment I Saw This Gorgeous Lake Como Airbnb, I Knew I Had to Strategy a Trip to Perledo

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that maybe it’s because I’m a dreamer, or maybe it's because I’m slightly impulsive, but whenever I'm planning a trip, I start by browsing Airbnb.
  • For a stay in Italy, if it’s sleek, minimalist, or modern, keep it away from me.
  • Industry observers note that my family and I arrived in Lake Como on a scorching August day after spending seven days in Sardinia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that maybe it’s because I’m a dreamer, or maybe it's because I’m slightly impulsive, but whenever I'm planning a trip, I start by browsing Airbnb. I find it the easiest way to envision my time away, and I dropped the notion a long time ago that you don’t actually spend time in your accommodations. That's how I ended up finding myself in a teeny town called Perledo this past summer—my mom had always dreamed of visiting Lake Como for her birthday, so I decided to see what great accommodations I could find in the area for a visit in August, her birth month.

For a stay in Italy, if it’s sleek, minimalist, or modern, keep it away from me. I’m drawn to homes that feel like a reflection of the country I’m in—something uncommon with character and a story. So when I found this unbelievably charming rental in Perledo—a quiet village in the hills above Varenna, overlooking Lake Como—on the Airbnb platform, I booked it for my mom, sister, and I before we even had flights. I mean, look at it!

Industry observers note that my family and I arrived in Lake Como on a scorching August day after spending seven days in Sardinia. After a flight, bus, train, and short taxi ride up and around the mountain, we were thrilled to land in our newly introduced home. A few days before our arrival, our host, Giulia (having the same name as her felt like a good omen to me!), helped us navigate getting to the apartment from the train, offering us multiple numbers for local taxis, as we hadn't wanted to rent a car. (I'm glad we went that route, because I wouldn't have wanted to deal with parking.).

Recent findings suggest that upon entering the home, after several trips up and down the stairs, we threw down our bags and immediately made our way onto the balcony. The sunlight beamed through the French doors with the mountains in the background, and the smell of crisp Alpine air made the three of us pause. Staring at the boats as they glided through the water, we all immediately forgot about the long journey it took to get there.

We discovered a bottle of red wine, taralli, and a bunch of Nespresso pods waiting for us on the kitchen table, and I was delighted to find the pantry filled with essentials—salt, pepper, olive oil, and vinegar. You know, those items you might need to complete a meal or a snack, but are annoying to buy on vacation.

It has been revealed that the apartment felt warm from the sunlight, but also by design. The pearly walls, with green cabinets and warm wood accents, felt very grounding, like an extension of the atmosphere outside. The tile flooring in the living area reminded me of my cousin's house in Rome, and the pistachio-green-framed window in the bathroom opened wide for a clear picture of the mountains and lake.

Sources indicate that after already spending a week with my mom and sister, I was ready for some space, so I opted for the sofa bed with a memory foam topper in the living room. The bed was already made, so it was easy to slip into the soft sheets for a nap after my shower. Throughout the stay, we were mindful not to let the hot water meter fall below a certain level, per Giulia's advice, but between the three of us, we rarely came close.

Giulia also gave us tons of information about the area, including ferry schedules, walking paths, and numbers for hairstylists (I'm always looking for a good blowout). Being able to communicate with her as a local resource felt like we had a personal tour guide with us at all times.

When we left the apartment on our first evening, we followed Giulia’s instructions to catch the complimentary Perledo Night Bus, a service provided by the town from 7 p.m. till midnight, to get to nearby Varenna, where we could grab the ferry to take us to other towns. Walking up and down the mountain, especially at night, would have been challenging and slightly dangerous, so we were happy to grab the shuttle, which was a 10-minute walk from our place.

In a recent development, unlike Como town or Bellagio, Varenna is quieter, with restaurants that shut down around 9 p.m. Luckily, there are some places to eat and drink in Perledo too. For example, Bar Milano is where locals congregate for their morning espressos or evening nightcaps. For us, it was where we would grab our bus rides up and down the mountain, as well as breakfast (the apricot croissants are incredible).

The walk to Bar Milano was a deeply scenic experience for us—the sunlight glistening on the lake to our right; the lush green mountains dotted with homes to our left. We often noticed fountains and shrines to pray at on our journeys up and down, something consistent on most streets in the village. After arriving home with our breakfast every day, we would start our mornings slow, sitting on the balcony with our espressos and cornetti, taking in the postcard-perfect views of the lake. We often noted hi to our neighbors just below us, families who were keen on enjoying the morning air too.

We made few plans for our days, except a reservation for my mom’s birthday lunch. We spent four hours indulging at Passalacqua, the boutique hotel in Moltrasio, and between the beauty of the space, the unhurried pace of the meal, and the kindness of the staff, it’s a memory we will all keep forever. Other afternoons were spent ferry hopping, exploring different towns. In Bellagio, it was imperative we walked down the most famous corridor—Salita Serbelloni. Filled with small artisanal shops and restaurants, it was here I bought a rosary necklace from a man named Filippo, the owner of Bellagio Upcoming Wave, a family business that has been in operation for over 100 years. He told me that he grew up above the building.

After days spent on our feet, ears buzzing from the large crowds, nothing was more serene than returning to the quiet of our apartment. Stepping off the shuttle and onto the street for our walk back to the Airbnb brought a sense of tranquility over our three days there, like we were truly going home. Being able to stare into the night sky, overlooking the stillness of the water while being hit with a slight breeze, offered a respite from the adventures of the day.

Sources indicate that when I think of Lake Como, I think of two things: romance and luxury. Away from the noise but still close enough to the action, this Airbnb gave us a slice of that fantasy. I now recommend Perdolo to everyone. Safe to say, I’ll continue building my trips around great Airbnbs. The rest always figures itself out later.

Industry observers note that as the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#23. Chase’s New $350 IHG Card Offers 200,000 Points—Plus $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 36 min read (7148 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

Chase’s New $350 IHG Card Offers 200,000 Points—Plus $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
  • The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (See rates and fees).
  • Industry observers note that chase’s new $350 annual fee IHG credit card can return $400 in flight credits before your first renewal, on top of a 200,000-point initial bonus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (See rates and fees).

Industry observers note that chase’s new $350 annual fee IHG credit card can return $400 in flight credits before your first renewal, on top of a 200,000-point initial bonus. It also gives you enough elite nights to choose a confirmable suite upgrade without first earning those nights through hotel stays.

I covered the changes to Chase’s IHG card portfolio earlier, but the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card deserves a good look. I’ve generally thought of IHG cards as something to get for the bonus and keep for the benefits. This one gives me a reason to consider putting some spending on it, too.

And Chase confirmed to me that its elite nights stack with those from other IHG cards. For someone who already has both the Premier and Business cards, adding Premier Select means 50 annual elite nights total starting with the existing cards’ January 2027 deposits which is enough to choose hotel lounge membership without stays or spending.

The launch offer lets you earn 200,000 IHG points after $5,000 in purchases within three months of account opening. At my half-cent valuation, the 200,000-point bonus is worth $1,000. Having another IHG personal or business card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The published restriction applies to current holders of this particular card, and previous holders who received its fresh cardmember bonus offer within the past 24 months. Chase told me that 5/24 applies. How To Get $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline. Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute. That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard. The Free Night And Hotel Dining Benefits Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. The timing is different for new accounts: cards opened on or after October 1 qualify for their opening credits now. Existing accounts receive their first annual deposits in January. And the spending counters stay separate—$3,000 on one card and $2,000 on another won’t combine into a $5,000 block that earns two nights. $15,000 In Spending Is More Interesting Than It First Looks The card earns 12 points per dollar at participating IHG hotels, 6 on dining and other travel, and 3 on other purchases. At half a cent per point, those are returns of 6%, 3% and 1.5%. Chase’s advertised “up to 28X” at IHG includes base hotel program earnings and the Platinum bonus not just the rewards for credit card spend. But there are spending rewards that change the calculation. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Travel is sold in pieces. Guests experience it as one trip. When a flight delay knocks out the connection, the first hotel night, and the plans after it, guests expect someone to help put it back together. That’s travel’s accountability gap.

Industry observers note that disruption has become the real test of loyalty, and a chance for hotels to build it beyond points. Matt Miller of Marriott International and Lindsay Tuhey of Allianz Partners join Skift to break down how hotels can support guests across the whole trip and keep ownership of the relationship.

Tags: allianz partners, disruption, loyalty, marriott international, partner content, Skift Studio, Skift Studio Showcase: Hospitality, webinar.

It has been revealed that skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Industry observers note that skift is hosting a webinar with Matt Miller of Marriott International and Lindsay Tuhey of Allianz Partners on what the session calls travel's accountability gap: travel is sold in pieces, but guests experience it as one trip, and when a flight delay knocks out a connection, the first hotel night, and the looks after it, guests expect someone to help put it back together. The session frames disruption as the real test of loyalty, and as a chance for hotels to build loyalty beyond points. The agenda covers where to focus 2027 loyalty investment as flexible cancellation, points, and status lose their pull; what guests need when a trip goes wrong, from medical help abroad to coverage for everyone in the room; whether travel protection belongs in the hotel booking path; which guest moments are too high-stakes to automate; and how to structure a protection partnership so the guest relationship stays with the hotel brand.

Industry News: A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app.
  • In a recent development, case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just introduced.
  • Sources indicate that british Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

In a recent development, case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just introduced. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

Sources indicate that british Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows….

It has been revealed that as noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Sources indicate that avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

In a recent development, I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

In a recent development, yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#20. Industry News: What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

Industry News: What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges.
  • I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.
  • Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:.

So unless you’re looking to chow down or drink up, you’re generally going to find more comfortable accommodations in the terminal. And before someone notes “you’re so obsessed with privacy,” let me point out my biggest problem with crowding — it’s that there’s invariably going to be someone within earshot making a phone call or watching something without headphones.

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):.

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:.

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

Industry observers note that my expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

According to recent reports, what sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:.

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

In a recent development, what sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):.

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

In a recent development, we’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

According to recent reports, I mentioned an interesting flag pin in my account of our excellent SAS Business Class flight from Chicago to Copenhagen. Here is the story.

It has been revealed that the purser was working my side of the aircraft, and I noticed a Greenland flag pinned to his uniform. Naturally, I was curious, especially considering I had just been there.

“To send a statement, especially on flights to the U.S.”.

Let me be clear: I find the Trump administration’s saber-rattling over Greenland among its most offensive actions.

In a recent development, denmark is a NATO ally. Threatening to take control of territory within the Kingdom of Denmark is an appalling way to treat a partner. Sometimes the only way to deal with a bully is to stand up to him.

Thankfully, diplomacy has produced a more constructive path. The United States, Denmark, and Greenland signed a security agreement in September that recognizes Danish sovereignty and Greenlandic self-determination while strengthening Arctic security.

Our flight took place before Greenland’s parliament ratified the agreement on November 3. Denmark’s parliamentary vote is scheduled for November 19, so the ratification process is not yet complete.

According to recent reports, I cautiously welcome that progress. Cooperation with an ally should have been the approach all along.

Here, however, I did not have to speculate about his intent. I asked, and he told me. He wanted to send a message, particularly to an American audience.

Industry observers note that sorry, but I take issue with that. Just wear the uniform as prescribed so everyone looks…uniform. The airline should determine what belongs on it. Individual employees should not decide which geopolitical causes deserve an exception.

Industry observers note that I have not established whether SAS permits this particular pin, so I am not claiming a confirmed uniform-policy violation. My objection is to using the uniform for the purpose he described.

This did not change my assessment of the flight. We enjoyed excellent food, slept very well, and received attentive service. I have already praised the crew, including this purser who made a great cappuccino, and that praise stands.

Recent findings suggest that but it is worth discussing precisely because I sympathized with him. Consistency is easy when you dislike the message. The more useful test comes when someone expresses a view you share. If I want political advocacy kept off crew uniforms, that has to apply here too. Otherwise, my position amounts to allowing the messages I like while objecting to everyone else’s.

My SAS purser wore a Greenland flag pin and openly acknowledged that he wanted to make a statement, especially on flights to the United States.

In a recent development, I understood his frustration and agreed with the underlying sentiment. I still do not think his uniform was the right place to express it. He helped deliver an excellent flight. I would happily fly with him again, but hopefully next time he’ll leave his Greenland pin at home.

9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche
