💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury.
  • As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.
  • A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain.

“I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook.

In a recent development, “I’m in love with Erin French’s fresh cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne.

The seafood platter at the fresh Casa Juani in Boulder.

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish.

Industry observers note that “I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best Fresh Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City.

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author.

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals.

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan.

In a recent development, “Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City.

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez.

In a recent development, “I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City.

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats.

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea.

According to recent reports, “Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food tech giant Queens.

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia.

Inspectors entered the closed former Hyatt Regency Dearborn and found families living upstairs. Hotel room doors on the property were chained and padlocked from the outside. Two days later, police searched. The families were gone. Officers closed the case after about a two hour search. On September 22, inspectors found, On the 12th floor: Dozens of people, including young children, with groceries, suitcases, puppies and dog feces. On the 10th floor: Doors chained and padlocked from outside, apparently impossible to unlock from within. In a hallway: Packaging for a large machete (though no machete was seen). A project manager initially suggested a worker’s family was visiting for lunch. A guard said up to 100 people had lived there over the previous year, and his bosses told him to ignore residents. The hotel’s owner denied knowing families were living there. Police said the locked rooms secured workers’ equipment and their search found no criminal activity, such as human trafficking. This is the Edward Hotel and Convention Center which once had a revolving restaurant and a monorail connection to Fairlane Town Center. It left Hyatt in 2012, and the city shut it down in 2018. The property was acquired in 2016 for $20 million. That owner faced criminal charges in Canada that were ultimately withdrawn. It was sold in 2021 in a forfeiture sale for $18.25 million. The buyer defaulted on the mortgage and in 2024 it was auctioned by the sheriff for $9.85 million, but apparently an auction of the distressed note and sheriff’s deed ended at $5.925 million. According to Dearborn City Council materials from October 2024, Hyatt had expressed interest in returning if sufficient capital investment could be secured. This exterior photo is from September 2024, by Warren LeMay via Wikipedia. But Wait, It Gets Worse According to a local activist a supposed immigration agent had thrown someone to the floor and killed a dog by throwing it through glass. She later reached an injured woman inside, who told her: “I don’t know how to get out.” The activist also said workers reported wages withheld because employers supposedly used the money to bribe immigration agents and being told: “Look, we’re keeping ICE away from you. Now you have to work for free.” Immigration and Customs Enforcement denies conducting enforcement at the hotel. A Detroit councilwoman’s office states Mayor Abdullah Hammoud was alerted September 18, four days before the inspection. Reportedly police failed to review the hotel’s surveillance video before closing the investigation. The Hotel Was Supposed To Make A Comeback Dearborn has sunk subsidies into the hotel’s redevelopment intends. In December 2025, the city approved a 12-year property tax exemption and a 30-year brownfield initiative for a redevelopment involving a $45 million rehabilitation, plus acquisition costs. The project would combine hotel rooms, apartments and convention space. In January, the mayor said the hotel would return as a Hilton, with a hoped-for opening by the end of 2026. Here’s a walk-through of the property from before the current state of affairs: I don’t think the former Hyatt Regency Dearborn is re-opening as a Hilton in 2026. It strikes me that the city isn’t adequately investigating problems at a redevelopment site that it’s subsidizing. #15. Breaking: White House Urges Congress To Approve $30 Billion In Upgrades To US Aviation Infrastructure

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words)
Business & Policy 🌐 Simpleflying

Breaking: White House Urges Congress To Approve $30 Billion In Upgrades To US Aviation Infrastructure

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The White House is urging Congress to approve an additional $30.1 billion for US aviation infrastructure upgrades.
  • The appeal comes as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has reportedly ordered a nationwide ground stop on November 13, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns.
  • Duffy and White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought have written to congressional leaders requesting swift approval of the additional investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The White House is urging Congress to approve an additional $30.1 billion for US aviation infrastructure upgrades. Reuters reports that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and budget director Russell Vought are pushing for action before Democrats take control of Congress in January. The request follows the Republicans' defeat in November's midterm elections, leaving the administration with a narrowing window to secure funding.

The appeal comes as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has reportedly ordered a nationwide ground stop on November 13, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns. The administration first requested approximately $30 billion in additional funding in September, on top of the $12.5 billion previously approved by Congress.

Duffy and White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought have written to congressional leaders requesting swift approval of the additional investment. With Democrats preparing to assume control of Congress on January 3, 2027, the administration is seeking to advance the proposal during the remaining weeks of Republican control. However, the legislation's prospects remain uncertain, and a change in congressional leadership does not necessarily mean the funding would be rejected.

Sources indicate that the administration argues that the funding is essential to replacing outdated air traffic control equipment, improving airport capacity, and strengthening the safety of the national airspace system. The latest proposal builds on a modernization program unveiled in 2025, following years of concern about aging communications infrastructure, controller shortages and operational disruptions. The investment is intended to accelerate upgrades that officials say cannot be completed with existing appropriations.

In their November 13 letter to Congress, Duffy and Vought said:.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace".

$12.5 billion in initial funding approved.

Duffy requests approximately $30 billion more.

It has been revealed that the funding campaign began well before this week's political developments. Duffy called for additional investment on September 22, shortly after a major Northeast air traffic control disruption. Senator Eric Schmitt subsequently introduced the Modern Skies Act on September 28, supported by major airlines and aviation industry organizations. The latest White House intervention represents a renewed effort to secure congressional approval rather than an entirely newly introduced funding initiative.

According to recent reports, the proposed investment would bring federal aviation modernization funding to approximately $42.6 billion, including the $12.5 billion originally approved in 2025. Unlike the earlier allocation, which concentrated on ATC improvements and controller recruitment, the latest request includes substantial funding for airports. Of the $30.1 billion, $18 billion would support airport infrastructure, including $10 billion to modernize or replace aging terminals.

ATC modernization, automation and cloud computing.

Replacement and improvement of ATC towers.

Airport infrastructure, including terminal modernization.

The FAA's infrastructure problems have accumulated over decades. Some facilities still depend on aging computers, with replacement components reportedly purchased through auction websites. The agency recently revealed intends to eliminate floppy disks used to distribute weather and other critical information at more than 400 ATC facilities by the end of 2028. These technological limitations have compounded existing concerns about staffing shortages, congestion and delays.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, modernization is already underway. According to Duffy, 68% of the FAA's legacy copper telecommunications network has been replaced with high-speed fiber infrastructure. The additional funding would accelerate upgrades to controller workstations, automation platforms and telecommunications, while expanding airport capacity. The challenge is implementing these improvements across one of the world's busiest aviation networks without creating further operational disruption.

A severed backup fiber line triggered ATC Zero conditions, grounding major Northeast airports and sending disruption toward Boston.

According to recent reports, the funding appeal coincides with an extraordinary disruption to US aviation. Earlier on Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, instructing departing aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice. According to Axios, the advisory cited "extraordinary circumstances and safety reasons," with international arrivals to be handled individually, although at the time of writing, the cause of the disruption had not been officially established.

In a recent development, the incident follows September's major Northeast ATC meltdown, when simultaneous telecommunications failures disrupted thousands of flights. A circuit failed at an air traffic facility in Philadelphia, while an Amtrak construction crew accidentally severed a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey. Ground stops affected several major airports, including Newark, Philadelphia and New York's airports, with knock-on delays extending to Boston.

Although the causes of today's nationwide ground stop still need to be established, the September incident demonstrated how communications failures can spread disruption across multiple airports. The FAA's modernization program aims to reduce these vulnerabilities through more resilient telecommunications, upgraded technology and improved infrastructure. With billions of dollars awaiting congressional approval, the latest disruption provides a timely backdrop to the administration's argument that further investment cannot wait.

US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations.
  • “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X.
  • Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”.

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”.

According to recent reports, the halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, stated that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. Newly introduced domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”.

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics manufacturer, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”.

In a recent development, the Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing flights across the U.S. to resume after halting takeoffs for several hours Friday evening.

But travelers will face significant disruptions through the weekend as airlines unwind one of the most significant disruptions to air travel in decades.

At 8:15pm EST, the FAA began allowing flights to operate, the Trump administration said. It came after a four-hour ground stop that stranded flyers at airports across the country.

Most departing flights in the U.S.were grounded indefinitely late Friday afternoon after the FAA reported communication complications impacting air traffic control centers.

The fallout for travelers was severe, affecting thousands of flights — a meltdown that was likely to cascade across multiple days.

More than 6,000 departures had been canceled as of 8:45 p.m. Friday evening, according to FlightAware. At least 1,400 departures for Saturday had been scrapped.

That number is likely to rise sharply as airlines work to get operations back on track.

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a news conference Friday evening.

Friday's communications outage occurred during an upgrade to FAA technology, officials said.

The disruption marked only the second time since 9/11 that a ground stop affecting the entire nation had been issued.

Airlines issued travel advisories in the midst of the travel chaos. These waivers typically allow passengers with flights booked more flexibility to change their itineraries:.

Some departures continued, despite the wide-ranging ground stop.

In a social media post, United Airlines noted international departures were being managed on a case-by-case basis, the carrier reported.

It has been revealed that alaska Air Group, which owns Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, said flights within the state of Alaska were still cleared to operate. Neighbor island service in Hawaii was also unaffected. Departures from the West Coast to Hawaii were also continuing, a spokesperson said.

Passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel or accept a rebooked flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption.

According to recent reports, under Department of Transportation rules, a significant delay generally means arriving at your final destination at least three hours late on a domestic itinerary or six hours late on an international itinerary. For passengers who decide to not travel on those flights, airlines must provide refunds to the original form of payment, not just travel credits.

In large-scale travel disruptions like this, rental cars and hotel rooms at or near airports can book up quickly, so it can make sense to act fast if you want to secure a backup option.

It has been revealed that if you have airline miles you can use to book a flight for tomorrow, that can also be a good self-insurance policy in case the disruption isn't resolved promptly. Just make sure you understand the cancellation and refund rules before booking a backup ticket.

In a recent development, and while many rewards credit cards offer built-in trip delay or cancellation protection if you used them to book your original airline tickets, it's not guaranteed that those benefits will cover FAA groundings of this nature. Still, save your receipts for any unexpected expenses in case you're eligible for reimbursement.

General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop, But The Airline Meltdown Is Far From Over

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the FAA halted departures nationwide Friday afternoon, November 13, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centers.
  • According to recent reports, that is welcome news for everyone waiting to travel.
  • During the evening press conference, Duffy attributed the disruption to aging air traffic control communications equipment that became overloaded with data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the FAA halted departures nationwide Friday afternoon, November 13, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed Friday evening that the system had reopened at 8:15 pm ET.

According to recent reports, that is welcome news for everyone waiting to travel. It does not, unfortunately, put aircraft and crews back where they need to be….

During the evening press conference, Duffy attributed the disruption to aging air traffic control communications equipment that became overloaded with data.

According to recent reports, homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted officials were also examining how older equipment interacts with newer technology. That, of course, is a preliminary explanation, not a completed technical investigation. We still await a detailed account of what triggered the failure and why the system could not absorb it without such an extraordinary interruption.

It has been revealed that duffy warned that restoring airline operations would take time. The government and airlines would try to move flights Friday night, with recovery efforts continuing Saturday.

Mullin offered a more reassuring assessment of the security question:.

“We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack.”.

There has also been speculation about the FAA’s newly introduced SMART traffic-management tool. Its developer, Air Space Intelligence, denied that its software or integration caused the ground stop.

I would wait for the technical findings before assigning blame to a particular product or contractor, though the timing is certainly suspicious.

It has been revealed that by 8 pm ET, FlightAware revealed more than 10,000 delays and 5,000 cancellations involving U.S. flights.

In a recent development, the operational problem is obvious: a flight that could not depart may leave another airport without the aircraft needed for its next departure. Crews can reach duty limits while waiting. Passengers miss connections, and the remaining seats fill swiftly.

Industry observers note that lifting the restriction allows airlines to begin untangling that mess, but of course does not instantly resolve it. Expect continued disruption tonight and check Saturday flights carefully too…this could go well into the busy Thanksgiving travel week.

In a recent development, the Department of Transportation explains that passengers are entitled to a refund when an airline cancels a flight and they decline the alternatives offered, regardless of the reason for cancellation. Qualifying significant delays also trigger refund rights when passengers choose not to travel.

Among the qualifying changes are scheduled arrival delays of at least three hours on domestic itineraries or six hours on international itineraries. You do not have to accept a voucher instead of a refund when a refund is owed.

That refund right is separate from whether the airline must pay for your hotel or dinner.

The FAA has lifted its nationwide departure restriction after a communications outage brought U.S. air travel to a halt Friday. Duffy pointed to overloaded older equipment, and Mullin stated there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Flights can resume, but the recovery will take longer. Check your individual itinerary, use any applicable waiver, and understand your refund rights before accepting an alternative that no longer works for you.

The FAA just froze every departure in the US over a communications failure at air traffic control centers. Here is what we know and what to do right now.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of alert nobody in travel wants to see on a Friday afternoon. The FAA has ordered a nationwide ground stop for every airport in the country, effective 3:54 p.m. Eastern, according to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center as reported by Gizmodo.

In a recent development, the notice to operators is blunt. It cites “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” and states “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice,” per WCVB. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis.

Aircraft already in the air are not being ordered down immediately and can continue to their destinations, according to Reuters reporting cited by IBTimes. The hold applies to departures.

In a recent development, transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the cause in plain terms on X: a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” He added that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” Those centers handle high-altitude, en route traffic across the country, so a problem there is not a local hiccup. It touches nearly every flight plan in the system.

There is one wrinkle worth flagging. An FAA spokesperson described the problem as affecting “multiple” centers, while Duffy said “all,” per Gizmodo. Just before the national order, both Chicago airports were placed under a ground stop for an “equipment outage,” according to NBC Chicago. The government has not provided further detail, and as of this writing (5:12pm EST) nobody official has said whether a cyber event has been ruled in or out. I would not speculate in either direction until the FAA does.

It has been revealed that the timing is awkward. Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize air traffic control communications, and the FAA and White House have asked for another $30.1 billion, as IBTimes notes. That money has not been applied to a solution yet so it’s unclear as to whether a future system would be able to avoid such a critical infrastructure system.

Sources indicate that extremely. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, according to the AP via ABC7. Reuters counts it as only the second nationwide halt of departures since September 11, 2001.

Sources indicate that that 2023 event came from the failure of the NOTAM system, which pilots rely on for safety notices. The FAA lifted that order just before 9 a.m. Eastern, but the damage was done: more than 3,700 flights were delayed and more than 640 canceled, per the AP report at the time. That stop hit on a Wednesday morning. This one hit a Friday afternoon heading into a weekend, with aircraft and crews about to be stranded out of position. Even a short pause will ripple into Saturday.

According to recent reports, for what it’s worth, SpaceX just started its launch channel ahead of a 5:45pm EST planned launch in which it will “double catch” both the booster and Starship. Space debuts likely have its own windows but cross shared airspace.

Recent findings suggest that if you are flying tonight, do not head to the airport on faith. Check your airline app first. Airports themselves are deferring to carriers, with Boston Logan telling passengers to “check with their airlines for the latest flight updates,” per WCVB. The Port Authority of Latest York and New Jersey could not even say whether planes were leaving JFK, according to Gizmodo. However, this amount of departures will take a long time to untangle and you’re unlikely to get out this evening.

According to recent reports, rebook if you can, and do it right now. The first people to grab the remaining seats on tomorrow morning’s flights are the ones who get out. If you have a cruise departure or a nonrefundable hotel tied to tonight’s flight, call the supplier now rather than after midnight. From the agency side, this is exactly when a travel advisor earns their keep, juggling the hotel, the ship, and the airline while you wait in line.

Sources indicate that keep your receipts for meals and hotels too. Airline policies on what they cover vary, and having the paperwork makes any claim easier. It’s unlikely the airlines will cover for an event out of their control but credit cards used to purchase this travel might.

A nationwide ground stop driven by a communications failure at the centers that run en route traffic is about as serious as an operational problem gets. The FAA has offered no time for departures to resume, and even when they do, Friday night’s schedule is effectively gone and Saturday will be messy. The bigger story will come after the planes are moving again: what failed, why there was no backup to keep traffic flowing, and whether the billions already earmarked for modernization are arriving fast enough.

We will update as the FAA and the airlines share more.

#9. Latest Update: How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15 min read (2955 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

Latest Update: How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt.
  • Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?
  • Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s crucial to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major matter you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

According to recent reports, the catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

It has been revealed that lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Recent findings suggest that note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

Sources indicate that you can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

According to recent reports, world of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

Industry observers note that it’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Sources indicate that hyatt acquired luxury travel manufacturer Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

In a recent development, while the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

It has been revealed that with the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Industry observers note that those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

It has been revealed that nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

In a recent development, world of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:.

In a recent development, even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:.

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

According to recent reports, as a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

Sources indicate that the reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:.

In a recent development, with World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no concerns redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Significant Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

According to recent reports, world of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Sources indicate that now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being remarked, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a roughly five-hour freeze on virtually all commercial aircraft departures, the FAA has lifted its nationwide emergency ground stop.

Industry observers note that the FAA canceled the ground stop around 8:20 p.m., and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed it at a press conference at the White House Friday night. He remarked it will take some time for flights to restart but emphasized that the air space is safe.

According to recent reports, according to Duffy, FAA personnel began to see inconsistencies in air traffic data around 3:30 p.m. Friday, and, out of an abundance of caution, the decision was made to ground flights not already in the air. He mentioned old analog ATC communications switches were overwhelmed and “went down,” causing the inconsistency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was triggered by an attempted technology update, which caused the system to reboot and crash.

There is no evidence of a cyberattack or terrorism, Mullin emphasized, and passengers were never in any danger.

In a recent development, duffy noted travelers should contact their airline for information about potential cancellations and delays. He said his department is in contact with the major carriers and will work with them to restore normal operations.

A small number of mostly international flights were cleared for takeoff at airports such as Fresh York-JFK, Washington Dulles, Reagan National, and Detroit Friday afternoon during the ground stop, but most remained grounded until the FAA reversed its order.

The FAA has ordered departures stopped at every U.S. airport after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers across the country. Planes are being held on the ground as Friday afternoon travelers head into the weekend, with no announced time for flights to resume. Aircraft already in the air are being allowed to continue and land. There isn’t a general order to put every plane down at the nearest airport, like 9/11. According to recent reports, there's often a lot of hype about the strategic benefits in a restructuring. Tripadvisor admitted its November 2025 restructuring didn't work.

According to recent reports, tripadvisor has unwound a 2025 restructuring that combined its “things to do” and Viator experiences teams under one roof. The two businesses are back to separate teams, similar to how they were organized before the November 2025 changes, according to a source familiar with Tripadvisor’s operations.

It has been revealed that under the new structure, Tripadvisor’s things to do business will have its own team. That business mainly generates leads for Viator, the company’s main experiences brand and the focus of its investment. Viator’s experiences operations will have a separate team.

In a November 4 internal email to employees, sent after an all-hands meeting at which outgoing CEO Matt Goldberg unveiled a firm-wide restructuring, Tripadvisor President Kristen Dalton wrote: “Experiences will be singularly focused on the Viator and Bokun brands with a focus on growth.” Bokun is Tripadvisor’s back-end reservations technology business for experiences operators, not a con.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

In a recent development, tripadvisor has reversed the November 2025 restructuring that merged its "things to do" and Viator experiences teams, returning to two separate organizations with, as President Kristen Dalton wrote to employees, "far less overlap between them and fewer shared services." The company told investors the combination "has not proven out as we expected": over the past 12 months, experiences booked through Viator and partner channels grew in the low teens while the Tripadvisor channel declined by high single digits, and third-quarter experiences revenue fell 3% year over year to $284.4 million. Tripadvisor noted November 5 it would cut 425 employee and contractor roles in its legacy Hotels & Other segment — about 60% of roles dedicated to hotel metasearch, display and sponsored ads, flights, cruise, and car rentals — with about 150 moving to Viator and a net reduction of roughly 275 positions, or around 17% of the workforce according to the Boston Globe. Cruise Critic, which sources said is profitable, is shrinking by 60% to around 20 employees, with all but one editorial staffer gone. The restructuring is expected to save about $40 million a year against $15 million to $20 million in charges, and it lands amid a leadership overhaul: CEO Matt Goldberg steps down in February, CFO Michael Noonan leaves December 31, and Dalton becomes interim CFO on January 1. Activist investor Starboard Value disclosed a 9% stake in July 2025 and gained four of 10 board seats in March; Tripadvisor has said no option is off the table for monetizing Viator.

  • In a recent development, on the surface level, it seems like the US Navy committed a strategic folly when it decided to replace the venerable Grumman C-2A Greyhound carrier-onboard delivery plane with a Bell Boeing tiltrotor.
  • Sources indicate that however, there is a crucial caveat that made all the difference when America's Navy decided to trade in for a fresh cargo plane.
  • Recent findings suggest that fitting the colossal jet engine into the Greyhound would have required a ground-up redesign of the plane's fuselage, which would have been a massive investment in a nearly obsolete platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on the surface level, it seems like the US Navy committed a strategic folly when it decided to replace the venerable Grumman C-2A Greyhound carrier-onboard delivery plane with a Bell Boeing tiltrotor. The newer and totally different rotary-wing aircraft has 40% less total payload than the 1960s vintage fixed-wing tail-hook plane it succeeded.

Sources indicate that however, there is a crucial caveat that made all the difference when America's Navy decided to trade in for a fresh cargo plane. Unlike the Greyhound, the Osprey can carry the engine of the Lockheed Martin F-35C Lightning II. This is a vital mission in supporting the new USN Carrier Air Wing, which is now deploying the world's first carrier-capable stealth fighters in combat missions.

Recent findings suggest that fitting the colossal jet engine into the Greyhound would have required a ground-up redesign of the plane's fuselage, which would have been a massive investment in a nearly obsolete platform. Although the Navy did lose some raw payload capacity, it gained a massive amount of mission flexibility and the benefit of operational commonality with the US Marines.

Industry observers note that the USMC has a very large number of V-22 Ospreys, which are deployed daily aboard US Navy vessels. That makes maintenance and logistics much simpler, but also taps into a skill pool of technicians and aircrew that has been refined for two decades to make the Navy's transition smooth.

Beyond the Marine Corps connection, the Osprey fundamentally changed how a Carrier Strike Group handles logistics, moving the Navy away from rigid, predictable Operations. The C-2 Greyhound was bound to the aircraft carrier's Flight Deck and airfields on the shore for every mission. If a C-2 Greyhound needed to pick up supplies near a conflict zone, it required a long, secure, paved military runway ashore.

The CMV-22B eliminates the middleperson. It can fly parts, mail, or personnel from a shore base directly to a destroyer, cruiser, or amphibious assault ship. It can also land on dirt fields, beaches, open drop zones, or small helicopter pads ashore to retrieve critical supplies or evacuate wounded personnel.

It has been revealed that additionally, the Osprey has a refueling probe that allows it to perform air-to-air refueling and extend its mission radius, which the Greyhound was never upgraded to receive. Another game-changing advantage is night operations. The Navy considered the aging C-2 Greyhound too risky for routine night landings on carriers. The CMV-22B, equipped with modern night-vision systems and avionics, can land vertically on a carrier's pitch-black deck at midnight, giving the fleet a true round-the-clock supply chain.

In a recent development, superior night ops capability significantly improves the operational flexibility of not only Air Wing but also the entire Carrier Strike Group. More than that, the latest ability is a force enhancement to the entire coalition as the US Armed Forces pivot to the Pacific with a focus on joint domain operations in a distributed battle space.

Likewise, the ability to resupply forces on remote islands without an airstrip is crucial in the Indo-Pacific. And the ability to perform aerial refueling will make the aircraft not only more practical but also enhance the safety of flight operating over vast expanses of open ocean.

It has been revealed that refocusing on the core capability that spurred the decision to make the transition to the COD mission, the capability to receive replacement engines for the Air Wing aircraft is crucial in a conflict. The Navy does not usually ship the entire, fully assembled engine at once. Instead, they transport the core F135 Power Module. This is the heaviest and most critical component of the engine.

It is, in fact, so heavy that the Osprey cannot perform a pure vertical lift but must execute a short rolling takeoff to get airborne. The C-2’s cabin is too narrow and awkwardly shaped to clear the engine's widest components. The Osprey's cargo bay can physically encompass these dimensions, but it leaves absolutely zero margin for error.

The engine module is mounted to a low-profile, heavy-duty wheeled metal frame that is compatible with a custom-designed skin rail system. The cargo crew pushes the module up the rear ramp, and it locks directly with the cargo floor's locking points to ensure the massive 3,750-lb (1,701 kg) powerplant cannot move during flight. While the engine technically fits, the tight clearance forces the Navy to accept unique operational compromises.

It has been revealed that because the module takes up nearly every cubic inch of the cargo bay, loading and unloading are a slow, meticulous process. Additionally, the F135 engine inside its standard shipping container will not fit inside the Osprey. Consequently, the engine must be flown 'naked,' or loosely wrapped. Ultimately, although it may not be the perfect transport option, it is the best available for the US Navy to sustain its fifth-generation Air Wing in the 21st century.

The legacy behind the latest and greatest Army helo.

Industry observers note that the absolute cornerstone of the fifth-generation air wing is the F-35C Lightning II, which has just one powerplant. If an F-35C suffers an engine failure out at sea, that multi-million-dollar stealth fighter is completely useless until a replacement arrives. This is especially critical as the aircraft is a single-engine airframe.

While the F135 is the most powerful fighter jet engine ever made, the fact that the F-35C only has one is a major departure from the recent portfolio of carrier-capable aircraft flown by the USN and USMC. The F-35C is vastly more maintenance-intensive than the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

The Legacy 4.5-generation Strike Fighter will be the support platform that continues to be the workhorse of the Air Wing, while the Joint Strike Fighter takes over the highest-risk missions like penetrating integrated enemy air defenses. To achieve supersonic speeds without a twin-engine layout, the F135 engine operates under extreme temperatures and pressures.

It generates massive electrical power to feed the jet's advanced radar, jamming systems, and electronic warfare sensors. In fact, the entire F-35 fleet of all variants around the world has suffered a critical readiness issue, and the latest upgrade package under Technology Refresh Three, Block Four, has been significantly delayed.

Despite the US Navy pumping nearly 1 billion dollars into a Lockheed Martin contract for advanced electronic warfare equipment, it doesn't solve the problem that these aircraft are more delicate, and working on them on the ship is far more burdensome as well.

The dynamic duo of America's carrier air wings.

The F-35C is built to strike targets deep inside enemy territory while the aircraft carrier stays positioned safely outside the range of land-based anti-ship missiles. This means the carrier operates much farther out to sea than it did in previous decades. The Osprey will liberate the logistical chain of the carrier strike group from airfields ashore and also improve the efficiency of operations to smaller vessels in the CSG.

Sources indicate that this is thanks to the fact that the CMV-22B can perform vertical resupply to smaller vessels as well. The Navy variant of the Osprey features massive fuel bladders bulged into the sides of the fuselage. It can fly over 1,150 nautical miles (2,130 km) on a single internal tank of fuel.

Unlike the old Greyhound, the Osprey features an aerial refueling probe. It can take fuel directly from F/A-18 'Buddy tankers' or the upcoming Boeing MQ-25 Stingray drones, which will take over air-to-air refueling for the Air Wing. Aerial refueling gives the Osprey virtually unlimited range, allowing it to fetch an urgent F-35C engine core from a distant shore base and sprint back to a fast-moving strike group without stopping.

Even more importantly, with the entire US Armed Forces concentrating their strategic disposition in the Pacific, the Osprey supports Joint Forces as a whole because it is engineered for the theater, and it can carry the engine of the most important fighter jet for virtually every operator in the region.

Out with old, in with the fresh for the USMC, but what's the catch?

In a recent development, the Indo-Pacific is an F-35 theater. The Air Force flies the F-35A from mainland bases, the Marines fly the short-takeoff/vertical-landing F-35B from amphibious ships and austere islands, and the Navy flies the carrier-borne F-35C. Crucially, all three variants of the F-35 use the same foundational Pratt & Whitney F135 engine core.

Recent findings suggest that because the Navy’s CMV-22B can haul this engine, it doesn't just service aircraft carriers. A Navy Osprey can fly an engine from a remote Air Force base in Guam, land on an amphibious assault ship, or drop it off at a rugged island outpost. In the vast Pacific, the Navy doesn’t have to build its own dedicated maintenance hubs on every island.

Sources indicate that the military knows that in a conflict, large, centralized bases like Kadena Air Base in Japan will be targeted by enemy ballistic missiles. To survive, the branches have developed decentralized strategies. Under modern Pacific strategy, a 100,000-ton Nimitz- or Ford-class aircraft carrier does not just exist to launch its own planes. It acts as a massive, floating logistical mothership for the entire joint force.

Recent findings suggest that in a shooting war, if a Marine or Air Force F-35 engine fails on a forward island outpost, the Navy's CMV-22B can lift a spare engine directly off the supercarrier's deck or from any depot in the first or second island chain operated by the US or its regional allies. It can then fly it directly to that carrier, 'Substantial Deck' assault ship, or tiny island airstrip.

Then the Osprey can land right in the dirt next to the stranded jet. It allows all of the US Armed Forces, Japanese, Australian, South Korean, Singaporean, and other regional military allies to pool their resources dynamically, thanks to the universal platform of the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter.

FAA Challenges Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

  • Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented.

  • In a recent development, DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control concerns in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:.

In a recent development, DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

In a recent development, as of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having challenges, prior to this going nationwide.

It has been revealed that kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies….

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All….

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”.

Industry observers note that the @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major glitch when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the fresh AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Sources indicate that timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication problems, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications matter, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q.

Recent findings suggest that one can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin remarked the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz.

Recent findings suggest that if this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that concern, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

According to recent reports, it remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

According to recent reports, this is only the third nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The last one, during a 2023 system outage, lasted about two hours.

The Federal Aviation Administration ended a nationwide ground stop Friday night more than four hours after a communication glitch affected the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the high-altitude air traffic control facilities that manage flights between airports.

The ground stop was lifted at around 8:15 p.m. ET, but disruptions are expected to linger into the weekend.

As of Friday night, there were more than 5,700 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware. Airlines have started canceling flights for Saturday, tallying to 980.

During a televised briefing Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack.

In a recent development, transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at 3:36 p.m. ET the FAA started "experiencing instability" at radar and communication at air traffic control centers and TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Controls). He said 3,500 planes were in the air at the time.

The FAA halted all departing flights across the U.S. on Friday after a communication glitch affected every Air Route Traffic Control Center, the high-altitude facilities that manage flights between airports, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy said on X that the agency "issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," and that FAA technicians are investigating. The agency said all departing flights would be grounded and inbound international flights would be handled case by case, citing "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare: the FAA issued one on 9/11 after the terror attacks, and again in January 2023 over problems with a pilot alert system. The story is breaking, and the FAA has not said how long the stop will last or what caused the communication failure.
